War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint. China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a series of export controls issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend – at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very big stick . California’s Mountain Pass mine led world production of rare earths until the late 1980s . Multiple instances of radioactive wastewater spilling from the mine into the Mojave Desert made it hard to keep domestic production running. When China expanded its own mining and sold the processed materials for less, the logic of switching rare earth suppliers was easy. Mountain Pass’ separation plant closed in 1998 , and the mine itself stopped in 2002. MP Materials restarted mining there in 2017 as concern about access to rare earth minerals rose, but the U.S. still imported more than two-thirds of the rare earth elements it used as recently as 2025. China, which mined about 60% of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about 91% of separation and refining . Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising. The U.S. Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years . Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons. China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the U.S. has far fewer experts . Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023. The U.S. government has committed more than US$7 billion since April 2025 to try to rebuild U.S. rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought $400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials in 2025, giving it 15% ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028. The Commerce Department also signed a letter of intent in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma. But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult. On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures . One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up 0.1% or more of its value , or if it used Chinese rare earth technology. After President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping that month , Beijing suspended six export controls until Nov. 10, 2026 , in exchange for Washington pausing its “ affiliates rule ,” which imposes restrictions on companies that are majority-owned by certain blacklisted firms, for one year. Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses. Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the heavier rare earths . Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets – critical to speakers and electrical motors – because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “ day to day ” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production only with Beijing’s approval . On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put 10 U.S. companies on its export control list . Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems and military vehicles. Two of them – MP Materials and USA Rare Earth – are the federally backed American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain. Beijing said its move was a response to a similar move by the Pentagon . My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing. An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice. For the U.S., leaving processing in China is the fastest and cheapest solution, but that leaves it exposed to Beijing’s restrictions . Rebuilding a U.S. rare earths supply chain would remove most U.S. dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars and separation produces acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues . Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the U.S. being cut off unilaterally. Japan has run this play with some success , but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad. extraction.body: At the edge of California’s Mojave Desert, the Mountain Pass mine looks like any other stretch of dust and rock. But for decades, this lonely pit supplied the world with the rare-earth elements that make modern technology — and modern warfare — possible. In the 1980s, Mountain Pass was the beating heart of a quiet American advantage. The ore pulled from its depths yielded neodymium, lanthanum and cerium — metals that powered radar systems, early computer chips and the guidance of precision munitions. At its peak, the mine met nearly two-thirds of global demand. As environmental rules tightened and global prices collapsed under China’s state-subsidized production, the U.S. abandoned what had once been its mineral lifeline. And the world’s most powerful economy became dependent on a rival for the elements essential to its defense. CHINA'S RARE EARTH TECH OBSESSION ENSNARES US RESIDENT AS CCP LOOKS TO MAINTAIN STRANGLEHOLD "The Middle East has oil; China has rare earths," former Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping declared in 1987. Just as Arab nations turned oil wealth into global power, Beijing recognized the leverage it could gain by dominating the materials modern industry would only grow more dependent on. China now controls roughly 70 percent of global rare-earth mining and nearly 90 percent of refining — the most strategic and profitable step in the chain. The sell-off that changed everything The U.S. didn’t just lose ground in mining — it handed Beijing the technology that made rare earths valuable in the first place. In the early 1990s, a General Motors subsidiary called Magnaquench was producing 85 percent of the magnets used in precision-guided missiles and other defense systems. When GM sold the company in 1995 to a consortium that included two Chinese entities, the consequences were immediate. Within a year, the entire product line had been replicated in China, and the U.S. had lost its magnet-making process almost overnight. Center for Critical Mineral Strategy at SAFE, said the sale represented more than a bad deal — it was a strategic surrender. "We were focused on the internet and globalization, not on where our materials were coming from," she said. "Policy became episodic rather than strategic." China builds, America hesitates While Washington debated environmental rules and trade policy, China moved aggressively. "The United States had Mountain Pass and a few other capabilities tied to companies like GM," said Wade Senti, president of Advanced Magnet Lab. Meanwhile, China poured money into innovation, refining and manufacturing at a scale that far exceeded what we ever had." By the early 2000s, the U.S. mining and refining base had collapsed. Beijing not only mined the minerals but mastered the high-value steps that turned them into finished magnets — the core of everything from fighter jets to electric vehicles. "Between market forces and environmental restrictions … it's certainly led to a constraint with extracting resources," Senti said. Rare-earth elements now underpin nearly every modern weapons system. "They steer missiles, power radar and drive the night-vision goggles Marines wear in the field," Hunter said. "If it moves, sees or communicates in today’s military, there’s probably a rare-earth element in it." A wake-up call from Beijing Washington’s complacency cracked this spring when Beijing briefly restricted exports of rare-earth products — a warning shot that rippled through supply chains from Detroit to the Pentagon. "When China required export licenses, some U.S. factory lines literally stopped," Hunter said. "The administration scrambled to negotiate with Beijing and simultaneously rolled out emergency support for MP Materials, the operator of Mountain Pass." That deal marked a turning point: for the first time, the federal government backed an entire supply chain — from mine to magnet — using every tool at its disposal. CHINA'S TRADE WAR WEAPONS: RARE EARTH BAN AND US DEBT DUMP COULD CRIPPLE AMERICAN ECONOMY AND DEFENSE MP Materials, which resumed mining at Mountain Pass in 2018 and ramped up refining to record levels before the Pentagon deal, is now expanding its magnet manufacturing facility in Texas. "It’s a ten-year project, not something we can do in a year," Hunter said. "We’re starting to see progress, but we’re nowhere near self-sufficiency." A global race for resources The Trump administration has put the U.S. on a wartime footing for decoupling with China, taking a 15 percent stake in MP Materials in an unprecedented arrangement and pushing a wave of international critical-minerals agreements meant to cut Beijing out of key supply chains. Over the past year, Washington has signed multi-billion dollar partnerships across five continents — including a $10 billion package of new projects announced this fall. A landmark framework with Australia commits both nations to co-invest roughly $1 billion each in rare-earth and battery-metal ventures, while parallel agreements with Japan and South Korea focus on securing non-Chinese refining and magnet production. Together, the web of pacts marks the most aggressive U.S. mineral diplomacy since the Cold War — a global race to control the elements that power modern weapons, vehicles and technology. Under a 2027 mandate, the Pentagon must build a fully domestic rare-earth supply chain for defense production — from mine to magnet — that avoids Chinese inputs entirely. Meeting that goal will require more than foreign partnerships: it means breaking through America’s own permitting gridlock, financing new refineries and rebuilding a skilled workforce that vanished when the industry collapsed two decades ago. "The international deals may buy time," Senti said, "but they’re no substitute for restoring the industrial base that once made us the world’s undisputed source of strategic minerals." The race to rebuild Both Hunter and Senti see the next few years as decisive. The same materials that once powered America’s Cold War innovation now underpin China’s economic and military strength.

extraction.body: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too. YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest. Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos. On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S. Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns. The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.” “Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post . Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior. YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs , and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface. YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry : In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year. extraction.body: On September 23 , YouTube held its annual Made On event in New York City. If you’ve tuned into previous editions of YouTube’s product spiel, the headlines for the 2026 presentation may sound familiar. YouTube is bringing more AI-powered personalization to both creators and viewers, and new testing tools will optimize the platform’s videos across multiple formats. Creators are always looking for any slight advantage that can make their content stand out amid a noisy field. YouTube Studio is delivering that optimization in multiple ways. “YouTube Studio is evolving into an end-to-end creative partner to help across production, packaging, and channel strategy,” reads a Made On blog post attributed to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan . For starters, the platform is expanding the A/B tests it has been slowly introducing since 2023. Those experiments already allow creators to pit multiple titles and thumbnails against each other to determine which one performs better. Soon, that process will expand to entire videos. By A/B testing multiple cuts of the same clip, creators can identify the version that best resonates with their audience. Those tests can locate what YouTube calls “outlier videos”: exceptional performers that can inspire future uploads. New Insights and Research data in YouTube Studio can add more context to those outliers, and the same philosophy is being applied to thumbnails, too. After bringing dynamic insertion to its ads at last year’s Made On event, YouTube is now introducing dynamic thumbnails. By automatically switching between multiple preview images, YouTube is aiming to maximize reach among specific audience segments. As part of its Made On pitch, YouTbe alluded to its first-ever GenAI trends report , which found that 72% of U.S. video uploaders between the ages of 14 and 44 have used AI as a creative aid over the past year. AI suggestions delivered by Google’s Gemini models are saving time for users while turning YouTube into a more targeted experience. If you think AI-powered personalization is already ubiquitous on YouTube, just wait. As we learned at Made On, YouTube is finding more ways to tailor its design to individual users. For social shoppers, an expanded Ask YouTube feature will turn questions and follow-ups into interactive product recommendations that show up across TV and mobile surfaces. And to improve a destination Mohan called “the #1 podcast platform for viewers in the US,” YouTube is building personalized podcast lineups that reflect each listener’s tastes and interests. A similar mechanism is coming to YouTube’s homepage. At Made On, Mohan officially announced the new Custom Feeds . That tool can turn users’ suggestions into fully populated landing pages that cut across specific content categories. “Custom Feeds allows you to create dedicated tabs for any interest, routine, or mood,” said video essayist Mina Le at the Made On event. “Just prompt a new feed into existence and it appears right there on your homepage, constantly updating with hyper-relevant creators and content.” In other words, YouTube homepage shelves will now deliver the granular recommendations Netflix users have come to expect. But YouTube’s copycat approach doesn’t stop there. Made On YouTube 2026 shows that Mohan and his deputies are paying attention to the formats, features, and products that are shining on other platforms. A lot of that has to do with AI; YouTube, like Spotify, wants to automate audio recommendations, which is why it’s bringing Ask Music — its version of the Spotify DJ — to the YouTube Music app. When it comes to TikTok, however, YouTube is borrowing much more than just AI-powered updates. It is leaning into the growing popularity of microdramas by expanding its Series feature . TikTok has found ways to monetize serialized short-form collections , and YouTube is taking a step in that direction with the introduction of Shorts Series . The sequential short-form playlists will build on YouTube’s current microdrama momentum, which includes more than six billion views . Then, there’s the matter of TikTok LIVE, a popular vertical live-streaming format that has inspired Made On YouTube updates over the past three years. To make its own Vertical Live streams as functional as their TikTok analogues, YouTube is introducing several new broadcast options. Go Live Together will enable co-hosting on those streams, Live showdowns will turn them into collaborative fundraisers, and Live auto-dubbing will bring streaming content to viewers across the globe. All of those Vertical Live updates are due to arrive in “early 2027.” From that point on, YouTube has no plans to slow down. Instead, users can expect the flurry of new features to continue. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said at Made On. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era.” Stay up-to-date with the latest and breaking creator and online video news delivered right to your inbox.

The announcement represents significant developments for digital marketing strategies, particularly regarding creator partnerships and video advertising.

Enhanced targeting capabilities in YouTube Shopping align with broader programmatic advertising trends.
TikTok's Effect House and Instagram's AR tools provide comparable creation features, but lack the integrated monetization infrastructure YouTube offers through its Partner Program.
The combination of AI content creation with established revenue sharing creates competitive advantages for creator retention and platform loyalty.

YouTube revealed its most comprehensive creator toolkit at the Made on YouTube event on September 16, 2025. The announcements span artificial intelligence-powered content creation, enhanced monetization features, and significant live streaming improvements. According to Chief Product Officer Johanna Voolich, the platform has paid out $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies over the past four years.

The platform introduced Veo 3 Fast, a custom version of Google DeepMind's video generation model, integrated directly into YouTube Shorts. This marks the first time creators can generate video content with sound from text prompts directly within the platform. The feature launches initially in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, with expansion planned for additional markets.

YouTube integrated Google DeepMind's Lyria 2 music model through the Speech to Song feature. This tool converts dialogue from eligible videos into musical soundtracks for Shorts. Creators can specify musical styles including chill, danceable, or fun vibes while maintaining attribution to original content creators.

The platform expanded its AI capabilities with Edit with AI, which transforms raw footage into structured video content. The feature automatically arranges clips, adds music and transitions, and includes voiceover in English or Hindi. According to company documentation, this addresses creator challenges with blank timeline intimidation by providing solid starting points for content development.

YouTube Studio received comprehensive updates designed to function as a creative partner throughout the content creation process. Ask Studio introduces conversational AI for analytics insights, community understanding, and creative inspiration. Creators can ask questions like "catch me up on how my last video is performing" or "tell me what my community is saying about my editing style."

The Inspiration Tab received enhancements with suggested topics, creative direction building, and audience behavior insights. Title A/B testing expanded to support three title and thumbnail combinations per video, building on the thumbnail testing feature used over 15 million times since 2023.

Auto-dubbing capabilities gained lip sync technology to align translated speech with speaker mouth movements across 20 languages. The platform also expanded likeness detection tools to all YouTube Partner Program creators through open beta, helping detect unauthorized AI-generated content using creator facial likenesses.

extraction.body: YouTube is giving creators more tools to test, optimize and distribute their content as the platform expands its use of artificial intelligence across video creation and discovery. The company announced a series of new creator features on Wednesday, including AI-powered feedback through Ask Studio, video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, automated product tagging and real-time dubbing for live videos. The tools are designed to help creators understand what works on their channels, improve existing videos and reach audiences in more markets. YouTube is expanding Ask Studio, its AI assistant for creators, to mobile apps. The tool can analyse draft videos and provide personalised feedback based on a creator’s previous content and audience comments. It can also suggest alternative titles and thumbnails while analysing channel analytics to explain why particular videos performed the way they did. Ask Studio can then offer recommendations on how creators could improve their content and performance. YouTube is also extending some of these capabilities to older videos. With a creator’s permission, Ask Studio can monitor thumbnail performance and automatically create tests to determine whether different thumbnails improve how viewers respond to existing content. YouTube already allows creators to test different titles and thumbnails to determine which versions perform better. The company plans to expand this capability in 2027 by allowing creators to upload and test up to three different cuts of a Short. The platform is also introducing Dynamic Thumbnails , which allows creators to upload multiple thumbnails and lets YouTube determine which one to show to viewers based on which is most likely to generate interest. The feature could reduce the need for creators to manually monitor thumbnail performance and repeatedly change thumbnails based on analytics. However, the increased use of AI in content optimisation also raises concerns among creators who worry that inaccurate AI-generated suggestions could affect their credibility or misrepresent their content. For these tools to gain wider adoption, creators will need to trust that the recommendations and automated changes are accurate and aligned with their content. YouTube is also using AI to make video shopping easier for creators. The platform will automatically identify and tag products featured in videos, helping creators connect their content to affiliate opportunities and potentially earn commissions from product sales. YouTube is also expanding its Amazon affiliate programme beyond the United States. The changes come as the platform increasingly connects video discovery with shopping, allowing creators to turn product-focused content into another source of revenue. YouTube is expanding its live-streaming tools with features aimed at helping creators reach audiences beyond their primary language. Early next year, the platform plans to pilot automatic dubbing for live videos. The technology will translate a creator’s speech into other languages in real time, allowing viewers in different markets to follow live content in their own language. Real-time dubbing could make live streams more accessible internationally while allowing creators to reach audiences without having to produce separate versions of their content. The company is also launching a feature called Live Showdown , which will allow creators to co-host streams and compete against each other in real time. A related live creator matchmaking feature will pair creators with other creators who are currently streaming, creating opportunities for spontaneous collaborations. During a Live Showdown, viewers can support their preferred creator through chats, gifts and Super Chats, with the creator’s score displayed on screen in real time. The format gives YouTube another way to make live content more interactive while encouraging collaborations between creators. YouTube also shared new data showing how viewing habits are changing on the platform. More viewers are watching YouTube through household televisions, with more than half of the platform’s top 100 creators having the living room as their most-watched viewing interface. Short-form episodic content is also gaining traction. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube during the first half of 2026 , while watch time for the format increased 50% year over year. The growth is not limited to mobile devices. Views of microdrama content on televisions increased 90% year over year, suggesting that audiences are increasingly consuming vertical, episodic content on larger screens. The new features show YouTube’s broader effort to integrate AI into different stages of the creator experience, from developing content and choosing thumbnails to analysing performance, monetising videos and reaching international audiences. For creators, the tools could reduce some of the manual work involved in optimising a channel. But their success will also depend on whether creators trust AI to make recommendations and automated decisions without compromising the quality or authenticity of their content. As YouTube continues to expand beyond traditional video recommendations, the platform is positioning AI as a central part of how creators produce, optimise, distribute and monetise their work.

extraction.body: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best. The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too. YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest. Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos. On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S. Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns. The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.” “Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post . passages: In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best.

The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too.

YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest.

extraction.body: On September 23 , YouTube held its annual Made On event in New York City. If you’ve tuned into previous editions of YouTube’s product spiel, the headlines for the 2026 presentation may sound familiar. YouTube is bringing more AI-powered personalization to both creators and viewers, and new testing tools will optimize the platform’s videos across multiple formats. Creators are always looking for any slight advantage that can make their content stand out amid a noisy field. YouTube Studio is delivering that optimization in multiple ways. “YouTube Studio is evolving into an end-to-end creative partner to help across production, packaging, and channel strategy,” reads a Made On blog post attributed to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan . For starters, the platform is expanding the A/B tests it has been slowly introducing since 2023. Those experiments already allow creators to pit multiple titles and thumbnails against each other to determine which one performs better. Soon, that process will expand to entire videos. By A/B testing multiple cuts of the same clip, creators can identify the version that best resonates with their audience. Those tests can locate what YouTube calls “outlier videos”: exceptional performers that can inspire future uploads. New Insights and Research data in YouTube Studio can add more context to those outliers, and the same philosophy is being applied to thumbnails, too. After bringing dynamic insertion to its ads at last year’s Made On event, YouTube is now introducing dynamic thumbnails. By automatically switching between multiple preview images, YouTube is aiming to maximize reach among specific audience segments. As part of its Made On pitch, YouTbe alluded to its first-ever GenAI trends report , which found that 72% of U.S. video uploaders between the ages of 14 and 44 have used AI as a creative aid over the past year. AI suggestions delivered by Google’s Gemini models are saving time for users while turning YouTube into a more targeted experience. If you think AI-powered personalization is already ubiquitous on YouTube, just wait. As we learned at Made On, YouTube is finding more ways to tailor its design to individual users. For social shoppers, an expanded Ask YouTube feature will turn questions and follow-ups into interactive product recommendations that show up across TV and mobile surfaces. And to improve a destination Mohan called “the #1 podcast platform for viewers in the US,” YouTube is building personalized podcast lineups that reflect each listener’s tastes and interests. A similar mechanism is coming to YouTube’s homepage. At Made On, Mohan officially announced the new Custom Feeds . That tool can turn users’ suggestions into fully populated landing pages that cut across specific content categories. “Custom Feeds allows you to create dedicated tabs for any interest, routine, or mood,” said video essayist Mina Le at the Made On event. “Just prompt a new feed into existence and it appears right there on your homepage, constantly updating with hyper-relevant creators and content.” In other words, YouTube homepage shelves will now deliver the granular recommendations Netflix users have come to expect. But YouTube’s copycat approach doesn’t stop there. Made On YouTube 2026 shows that Mohan and his deputies are paying attention to the formats, features, and products that are shining on other platforms. A lot of that has to do with AI; YouTube, like Spotify, wants to automate audio recommendations, which is why it’s bringing Ask Music — its version of the Spotify DJ — to the YouTube Music app. When it comes to TikTok, however, YouTube is borrowing much more than just AI-powered updates. It is leaning into the growing popularity of microdramas by expanding its Series feature . TikTok has found ways to monetize serialized short-form collections , and YouTube is taking a step in that direction with the introduction of Shorts Series . The sequential short-form playlists will build on YouTube’s current microdrama momentum, which includes more than six billion views . Then, there’s the matter of TikTok LIVE, a popular vertical live-streaming format that has inspired Made On YouTube updates over the past three years. To make its own Vertical Live streams as functional as their TikTok analogues, YouTube is introducing several new broadcast options. Go Live Together will enable co-hosting on those streams, Live showdowns will turn them into collaborative fundraisers, and Live auto-dubbing will bring streaming content to viewers across the globe. All of those Vertical Live updates are due to arrive in “early 2027.” From that point on, YouTube has no plans to slow down. Instead, users can expect the flurry of new features to continue. “Since the start of the year, we’ve launched over 3,000 product updates and improvements, keeping up with evolving viewer tastes and increasing creator ambitions,” Mohan said at Made On. “This is what it looks like to innovate in the YouTube era.” Stay up-to-date with the latest and breaking creator and online video news delivered right to your inbox.

passages: The $100 billion creator payout milestone represents approximately 45% of YouTube's total advertising revenue over the four-year period, according to industry estimates.
This revenue sharing rate significantly exceeds traditional media industry standards where content creators typically receive 10-15% of advertising revenue.

YouTube Partner Program membership reached 3 million channels, with 700,000 joining over the past three years.
Gross Merchandise Volume through YouTube Shopping grew 5X year-over-year with over 500,000 creators enrolled globally as of July 2025.
The integration of Veo 3 Fast represents significant computational requirements for YouTube's infrastructure.
According to technical documentation, the system processes text prompts through Google DeepMind's neural networks while maintaining 480p output resolution to balance quality with processing speed.
The reduced latency design enables real-time content generation on mobile devices, requiring substantial backend optimization.
The announcement represents significant developments for digital marketing strategies, particularly regarding creator partnerships and video advertising.
PPC Land has extensively covered YouTube's expanding role in the creator economy , noting the platform's evolution from simple video hosting to comprehensive business infrastructure.
Other features deploy across all YouTube markets with varying timelines.
This marks the first time creators can generate video content with sound from text prompts directly within the platform.
The feature launches initially in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, with expansion planned for additional markets.
Creator economy growth impacts traditional advertising agency models as brands increasingly allocate budgets toward creator partnerships rather than conventional media placements.
PPC Land analysis shows creator content marketing receives 89% advertiser approval , with 44% of marketers planning investment increases.
Enhanced targeting capabilities in YouTube Shopping align with broader programmatic advertising trends.
TikTok's Effect House and Instagram's AR tools provide comparable creation features, but lack the integrated monetization infrastructure YouTube offers through its Partner Program.
The combination of AI content creation with established revenue sharing creates competitive advantages for creator retention and platform loyalty.
This tool converts dialogue from eligible videos into musical soundtracks for Shorts.

Meta's Reels platform competes directly in short-form video content but relies primarily on external AI tools rather than integrated generation capabilities.

Over 30% of daily logged-in viewers watched live content in Q2 2025 according to platform statistics.
New features include simultaneous horizontal and vertical streaming with unified chat, practice mode for new streamers, and AI-powered highlight extraction for Shorts creation.
The dynamic brand segment insertion feature addresses advertiser demands for campaign flexibility that competing platforms struggle to match.
Traditional social media sponsorships require permanent content integration, while YouTube's system enables post-publication modifications and market-specific targeting.
Creators can ask questions like "catch me up on how my last video is performing" or "tell me what my community is saying about my editing style."
Auto-tagging capabilities will identify and tag eligible products mentioned in videos, reducing manual creator workload.
Music features focus on fan engagement through YouTube Music integration.
Traditional production barriers that favored established creators or brands with larger budgets may diminish as text-to-video generation becomes accessible.

extraction.body: YouTube unveiled its largest creator features update at Made on YouTube 2025, introducing AI-powered content creation tools and marking $100 billion paid to creators over four years. YouTube revealed its most comprehensive creator toolkit at the Made on YouTube event on September 16, 2025. The announcements span artificial intelligence-powered content creation, enhanced monetization features, and significant live streaming improvements. According to Chief Product Officer Johanna Voolich, the platform has paid out $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies over the past four years. The platform introduced Veo 3 Fast, a custom version of Google DeepMind's video generation model, integrated directly into YouTube Shorts. This marks the first time creators can generate video content with sound from text prompts directly within the platform. The feature launches initially in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, with expansion planned for additional markets. YouTube integrated Google DeepMind's Lyria 2 music model through the Speech to Song feature. This tool converts dialogue from eligible videos into musical soundtracks for Shorts. Creators can specify musical styles including chill, danceable, or fun vibes while maintaining attribution to original content creators. The platform expanded its AI capabilities with Edit with AI, which transforms raw footage into structured video content. The feature automatically arranges clips, adds music and transitions, and includes voiceover in English or Hindi. According to company documentation, this addresses creator challenges with blank timeline intimidation by providing solid starting points for content development. YouTube Studio received comprehensive updates designed to function as a creative partner throughout the content creation process. Ask Studio introduces conversational AI for analytics insights, community understanding, and creative inspiration. Creators can ask questions like "catch me up on how my last video is performing" or "tell me what my community is saying about my editing style." The Inspiration Tab received enhancements with suggested topics, creative direction building, and audience behavior insights. Title A/B testing expanded to support three title and thumbnail combinations per video, building on the thumbnail testing feature used over 15 million times since 2023. Auto-dubbing capabilities gained lip sync technology to align translated speech with speaker mouth movements across 20 languages. The platform also expanded likeness detection tools to all YouTube Partner Program creators through open beta, helping detect unauthorized AI-generated content using creator facial likenesses. Follow on Google , Google News , X , LinkedIn , Mastodon , Bluesky , Facebook , or via RSS Live streaming received what YouTube describes as its largest update ever. Over 30% of daily logged-in viewers watched live content in Q2 2025 according to platform statistics. New features include simultaneous horizontal and vertical streaming with unified chat, practice mode for new streamers, and AI-powered highlight extraction for Shorts creation. The collaboration feature allows up to five creators on single videos, with content distributed across all participant audiences. Revenue attribution goes to the posting channel, while all collaborators benefit from expanded reach. According to Voolich, this formalizes longstanding creator collaboration practices with product support. YouTube Shopping gained AI-powered product identification and automatic timestamping. The system identifies optimal moments for product mentions and displays tags at peak viewer interest. Auto-tagging capabilities will identify and tag eligible products mentioned in videos, reducing manual creator workload. Music features focus on fan engagement through YouTube Music integration. New release countdowns and pre-save functionality launch later this year, allowing fans to prepare for album releases. extraction.body: YouTube is giving creators more tools to test, optimize and distribute their content as the platform expands its use of artificial intelligence across video creation and discovery. The company announced a series of new creator features on Wednesday, including AI-powered feedback through Ask Studio, video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, automated product tagging and real-time dubbing for live videos. The tools are designed to help creators understand what works on their channels, improve existing videos and reach audiences in more markets. YouTube is expanding Ask Studio, its AI assistant for creators, to mobile apps. The tool can analyse draft videos and provide personalised feedback based on a creator’s previous content and audience comments. It can also suggest alternative titles and thumbnails while analysing channel analytics to explain why particular videos performed the way they did. Ask Studio can then offer recommendations on how creators could improve their content and performance. YouTube is also extending some of these capabilities to older videos. With a creator’s permission, Ask Studio can monitor thumbnail performance and automatically create tests to determine whether different thumbnails improve how viewers respond to existing content. YouTube already allows creators to test different titles and thumbnails to determine which versions perform better. The company plans to expand this capability in 2027 by allowing creators to upload and test up to three different cuts of a Short. The platform is also introducing Dynamic Thumbnails , which allows creators to upload multiple thumbnails and lets YouTube determine which one to show to viewers based on which is most likely to generate interest. The feature could reduce the need for creators to manually monitor thumbnail performance and repeatedly change thumbnails based on analytics. However, the increased use of AI in content optimisation also raises concerns among creators who worry that inaccurate AI-generated suggestions could affect their credibility or misrepresent their content. For these tools to gain wider adoption, creators will need to trust that the recommendations and automated changes are accurate and aligned with their content. YouTube is also using AI to make video shopping easier for creators. The platform will automatically identify and tag products featured in videos, helping creators connect their content to affiliate opportunities and potentially earn commissions from product sales. YouTube is also expanding its Amazon affiliate programme beyond the United States. The changes come as the platform increasingly connects video discovery with shopping, allowing creators to turn product-focused content into another source of revenue. YouTube is expanding its live-streaming tools with features aimed at helping creators reach audiences beyond their primary language. Early next year, the platform plans to pilot automatic dubbing for live videos. The technology will translate a creator’s speech into other languages in real time, allowing viewers in different markets to follow live content in their own language. Real-time dubbing could make live streams more accessible internationally while allowing creators to reach audiences without having to produce separate versions of their content. The company is also launching a feature called Live Showdown , which will allow creators to co-host streams and compete against each other in real time. A related live creator matchmaking feature will pair creators with other creators who are currently streaming, creating opportunities for spontaneous collaborations. During a Live Showdown, viewers can support their preferred creator through chats, gifts and Super Chats, with the creator’s score displayed on screen in real time. The format gives YouTube another way to make live content more interactive while encouraging collaborations between creators. YouTube also shared new data showing how viewing habits are changing on the platform. More viewers are watching YouTube through household televisions, with more than half of the platform’s top 100 creators having the living room as their most-watched viewing interface. Short-form episodic content is also gaining traction. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube during the first half of 2026 , while watch time for the format increased 50% year over year. The growth is not limited to mobile devices. Views of microdrama content on televisions increased 90% year over year, suggesting that audiences are increasingly consuming vertical, episodic content on larger screens. The new features show YouTube’s broader effort to integrate AI into different stages of the creator experience, from developing content and choosing thumbnails to analysing performance, monetising videos and reaching international audiences. For creators, the tools could reduce some of the manual work involved in optimising a channel. But their success will also depend on whether creators trust AI to make recommendations and automated decisions without compromising the quality or authenticity of their content. As YouTube continues to expand beyond traditional video recommendations, the platform is positioning AI as a central part of how creators produce, optimise, distribute and monetise their work.

extraction.body: XRP News: Royal Bank of Canada, one of North America's five largest banks and a designated Global Systemically Important Bank, disclosed a position in the Bitwise XRP ETF through a Form 13F filing submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for the quarter ended March 31, 2026, acquiring 2,000 shares valued at approximately $30,000. The disclosure, citing CUSIP 09174F107, represents RBC's first reported indirect exposure to XRP through a regulated investment vehicle. This is not simply a small-cap allocation from a large balance sheet. It is a compliance-cleared signal from a G-SIB that altcoin-specific ETF products have crossed an institutional risk threshold. We suspect the significance of RBC's position lies not in its dollar size, $30,000 is a rounding error against a $570 billion AUM base, but in what clearing it required internally. G-SIBs operate under Basel III capital frameworks and stringent compliance review; any crypto-adjacent product must pass legal, risk, and regulatory scrutiny before appearing on a 13F. The fact that it did, at a major Canadian bank with deep correspondent-banking relationships, suggests that the jurisdictional uncertainty that once surrounded XRP and Ripple Labs has receded sufficiently for institutional compliance departments to approve exposure. That is a materially different environment than existed even eighteen months ago. The mechanism functions as follows: Section 13(f) of the Securities Exchange Act requires institutional investment managers with more than $100 million in qualifying assets under discretionary management to file Form 13F with the SEC within 45 days of each calendar quarter's end. The filing discloses long positions in U.S.-listed equity securities, including ETF shares, as of the quarter-close date; it does not capture short positions, derivatives, or non-U.S. holdings. RBC's filing for Q1 2026, therefore, reflects its held position in the Bitwise XRP ETF as of March 31, 2026, not necessarily its current exposure. The Bitwise XRP ETF (NYSE Arca: XRP) was created in November 2025 to provide investors with regulated access to XRP, the native asset of the XRP Ledger, without requiring direct custody. This is not simply a small-cap allocation from a large balance sheet. It is a compliance-cleared signal from a G-SIB that altcoin-specific ETF products have crossed an institutional risk threshold.

We suspect the significance of RBC's position lies not in its dollar size, $30,000 is a rounding error against a $570 billion AUM base, but in what clearing it required internally. G-SIBs operate under Basel III capital frameworks and stringent compliance review; any crypto-adjacent product must pass legal, risk, and regulatory scrutiny before appearing on a 13F.

The fact that it did, at a major Canadian bank with deep correspondent-banking relationships, suggests that the jurisdictional uncertainty that once surrounded XRP and Ripple Labs has receded sufficiently for institutional compliance departments to approve exposure. That is a materially different environment than existed even eighteen months ago.

passages: Crypto allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets, although most institutions allocated between 1% and 2%.
Exposure was spread across spot ETFs, direct ownership, venture investments and hedge funds.

Bitwise interviewed senior investment professionals responsible for crypto allocations at 15 large institutions, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, foundations and family offices.
The study is based on interviews with 15 institutions and does not represent a broad statistical survey of institutional investors.
Bitwise said some institutions use structures that do not appear in 13F filings, meaning public filings may understate overall institutional crypto exposure.
Institutional investors largely maintained or increased their crypto exposure through the latest market downturn, according to a new study from Bitwise Asset Management.
None reduced its allocation during the roughly 50% crypto market drawdown between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026, while several increased their exposure.

Whether for competitive reasons or reputational ones, most have historically avoided disclosing what they own—which means the public conversation about institutional adoption runs largely on inference. Over three months, Bitwise interviewed the senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions at 15 of the world's largest institutions: endowments, foundations, public pension funds, multi-family offices, investment consultants, sovereign wealth funds, and public companies. We asked what they hold, how much, why, and what would make them sell. Not one institution we interviewed reduced its allocation through the roughly 50% drawdown between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. passages: Top news and crypto talking points for the week ahead.

Institutions are generally reluctant to discuss their crypto positions. Whether for competitive reasons or reputational ones, most have historically avoided disclosing what they own—which means the public conversation about institutional adoption runs largely on inference.

Over three months, Bitwise interviewed the senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions at 15 of the world's largest institutions: endowments, foundations, public pension funds, multi-family offices, investment consultants, sovereign wealth funds, and public companies. We asked what they hold, how much, why, and what would make them sell.
Not one institution we interviewed reduced its allocation through the roughly 50% drawdown between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. Several bought more.
Every institution that owns crypto owns bitcoin—for nearly all, their first, largest, and longest-held position, and increasingly one they pair with gold.
Allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets, with most between 1% and 2%.
Not one investor named price as a reason they would sell. The stated triggers are thesis failure, regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis.
Allocation size tracks inversely with the number of people who must approve it. Family offices reported the highest allocations, sovereign wealth funds the lowest.
The common assumption is that institutions are the weak hands in a crypto drawdown. These interviews suggest the opposite.
For a deeper dive into institutional crypto adoption, and to understand why we expect a majority of institutional investors to hold crypto within five years, read the full report.

extraction.body: XRP News: Royal Bank of Canada, one of North America's five largest banks and a designated Global Systemically Important Bank, disclosed a position in the Bitwise XRP ETF through a Form 13F filing submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for the quarter ended March 31, 2026, acquiring 2,000 shares valued at approximately $30,000. The disclosure, citing CUSIP 09174F107, represents RBC's first reported indirect exposure to XRP through a regulated investment vehicle. This is not simply a small-cap allocation from a large balance sheet. It is a compliance-cleared signal from a G-SIB that altcoin-specific ETF products have crossed an institutional risk threshold. We suspect the significance of RBC's position lies not in its dollar size, $30,000 is a rounding error against a $570 billion AUM base, but in what clearing it required internally. G-SIBs operate under Basel III capital frameworks and stringent compliance review; any crypto-adjacent product must pass legal, risk, and regulatory scrutiny before appearing on a 13F. The fact that it did, at a major Canadian bank with deep correspondent-banking relationships, suggests that the jurisdictional uncertainty that once surrounded XRP and Ripple Labs has receded sufficiently for institutional compliance departments to approve exposure. That is a materially different environment than existed even eighteen months ago. The mechanism functions as follows: Section 13(f) of the Securities Exchange Act requires institutional investment managers with more than $100 million in qualifying assets under discretionary management to file Form 13F with the SEC within 45 days of each calendar quarter's end. The filing discloses long positions in U.S.-listed equity securities, including ETF shares, as of the quarter-close date; it does not capture short positions, derivatives, or non-U.S. holdings. RBC's filing for Q1 2026, therefore, reflects its held position in the Bitwise XRP ETF as of March 31, 2026, not necessarily its current exposure. The Bitwise XRP ETF (NYSE Arca: XRP) was created in November 2025 to provide investors with regulated access to XRP, the native asset of the XRP Ledger, without requiring direct custody. The fund holds physical XRP through The Bank of New York Mellon, which serves as custodian, an institution that has been building dedicated digital-asset infrastructure since at least 2021 and now services multiple U.S. spot crypto ETFs across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and select altcoins. The fund charges a management fee of 0.34% and had accumulated approximately $345–$360 million in assets under management as of mid-May 2026. It is necessary to flag the epistemic status of one detail here: RBC has made no public statement confirming the rationale for the position, and the 13F reflects a point-in-time snapshot that may not represent the bank's current view. passages: Top news and crypto talking points for the week ahead.

Institutions are generally reluctant to discuss their crypto positions. Whether for competitive reasons or reputational ones, most have historically avoided disclosing what they own—which means the public conversation about institutional adoption runs largely on inference.

Over three months, Bitwise interviewed the senior investment professionals responsible for crypto decisions at 15 of the world's largest institutions: endowments, foundations, public pension funds, multi-family offices, investment consultants, sovereign wealth funds, and public companies. We asked what they hold, how much, why, and what would make them sell.
Not one institution we interviewed reduced its allocation through the roughly 50% drawdown between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026. Several bought more.
Every institution that owns crypto owns bitcoin—for nearly all, their first, largest, and longest-held position, and increasingly one they pair with gold.
Allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets, with most between 1% and 2%.
Not one investor named price as a reason they would sell. The stated triggers are thesis failure, regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis.
Allocation size tracks inversely with the number of people who must approve it. Family offices reported the highest allocations, sovereign wealth funds the lowest.
The common assumption is that institutions are the weak hands in a crypto drawdown. These interviews suggest the opposite.
For a deeper dive into institutional crypto adoption, and to understand why we expect a majority of institutional investors to hold crypto within five years, read the full report.

sources.title: Ondas acquires three Israeli companies for $56 million as it builds autonomous defense stack
passages: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare.
The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock.
In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group.

Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year.

Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture.
Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms.
The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception.

Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution.
The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas.
Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally.
The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas.
The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk.

The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies.

extraction.body: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare. The acquisitions of Insignito, Ottopia Defense and Caribou Labs add capabilities spanning passive acoustic drone detection, resilient communications and remote control for unmanned systems, and navigation and communications in environments where GPS and other satellite-based systems are disrupted. The deals include additional contingent consideration of up to $32 million, payable if the businesses meet performance targets through 2028. The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock. Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year. The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas. The company has allocated restricted stock units representing 2,979,063 shares and options to purchase an additional 80,000 shares to the new employees. Taken together, the three acquisitions illustrate the kind of defense technology stack Ondas is attempting to build. Insignito adds another layer to the detection of unmanned aircraft, Ottopia provides the communications and human control needed to operate unmanned systems remotely, while Caribou addresses navigation, positioning and communications when conventional satellite signals are unavailable. Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture. The company says the three technologies range from systems already deployed in active conflict environments to capabilities that can be integrated into its existing platforms in the near term. Insignito, founded in 2022 by entrepreneurs with Air Force backgrounds, specializes in passive acoustic intelligence for counter-drone systems. The technology is designed to complement rather than replace other sensors, including radar, radio-frequency and electro-optical systems. The problem is becoming more significant as drones are increasingly used on battlefields and operators encounter systems designed to avoid traditional detection methods, including fiber-optic-controlled drones. Insignito has also developed several additional technologies around acoustic signatures. The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception. Ottopia Defense addresses a different problem: maintaining the connection between an unmanned vehicle and its human operators when battlefield communications become unreliable. The company develops software and communications infrastructure for transmitting video, telemetry, mission data and commands between unmanned maneuvering platforms, remote operators and command centers. Its system is designed for remote and bandwidth-constrained environments in which communications can be degraded or disrupted. It dynamically manages operational data across available communications channels, with the aim of preserving the flow of information between the vehicle and its operator. Ottopia combines AI-enabled autonomy with ultra-low-latency teleoperation and remote control. This allows operators to supervise multiple unmanned systems, monitor live video and telemetry, and intervene when human judgment or direct control is required. Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms. The acquisition therefore adds the communications and human-control layer to a broader portfolio of autonomous vehicles. Caribou Labs operates in deep tech, specializing in radio-frequency engineering, sensing, communications, positioning and timing for electronic-warfare environments. Its technology is designed to provide positioning and timing without relying on GPS and to maintain resilient communications when digital infrastructure or satellite-based navigation is disrupted. For autonomous systems, losing GNSS signals is not simply a communications problem: it can interfere with a vehicle's ability to determine where it is and how to navigate. Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally. Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution. The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas. The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies. In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group. Earlier this month, it agreed to acquire Israeli Gate Technologies and its Polish manufacturing partner, Bron Technologies, for approximately $205 million, expanding into electronic fuzing systems used in missiles, rockets, UAVs and loitering munitions. Ondas has also acquired U.S. defense technology company DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $876 million, its largest acquisition to date. The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk. The company has been financing the expansion alongside a rapid increase in revenue.

sources.title: Ondas and Heidelberg Establish ONBERG Autonomous Systems Joint Venture to Advance European Drone Defense Industry
passages: Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous aerial and ground robot intelligence through its Ondas Autonomous Systems ( OAS ) business unit and private wireless solutions through Ondas Networks, and Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG (FWB:HDD) ("Heidelberg"), a global leader in technology and mechanical engineering, today announced the formation of ONBERG Autonomous Systems ("ONBERG"), a joint venture with HD Advanced Technologies GmbH ("HDAT"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Heidelberg.

The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems.

"This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas.

extraction.body: Ondas ONDS said it has acquired DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $875 million, marking what Chairman and CEO Eric Brock described as a transformational step in building a scaled autonomous defense and security platform. Speaking on an investor event call, Brock said the deal includes $200 million in cash and approximately $675 million in Ondas equity. He said the acquisition closed concurrently with signing on July 2, allowing integration to begin immediately. DZYNE shareholders, led by majority owner Highlander Partners, will become among Ondas’ largest stockholders, and Highlander has locked up more than half of the shares it received for six months, according to Brock. “This is not a financial acquisition,” Brock said. “It is a strategic combination designed to create a larger, stronger, and more competitive autonomous defense company.” Brock said DZYNE brings operational products, a U.S.-based manufacturing base, customer relationships across defense agencies and allied militaries, and nearly 120 engineers. He said the acquisition expands Ondas’ position in persistent intelligence, aerial security, counter-drone systems, autonomous effects and AI-enabled mission intelligence. DZYNE’s portfolio spans three core franchises, according to the company presentation: Matt McCue, founder and CEO of DZYNE and incoming chief technology officer of Ondas Sentinel, said Ultra provides more than three days of endurance at more than 25,000 feet, while LEAP provides more than a day of endurance at 17,000 feet. He said both platforms are in operational use with U.S. and allied partners. McCue said IonStrike was developed from concept to demonstrated capability in six months to address threats such as the Shahed-136 drone. He also highlighted Dronebuster and Sawtooth as soft-kill counter-UAS systems, and said DZYNE is working on a long-range electronic attack solution and lidar detection capability. Ryan Hartman, CEO of Ondas Sentinel, said DZYNE fills a gap between Ondas’ lower-altitude unmanned systems and stratospheric assets, adding Group 4 and Group 5 long-endurance UAS capabilities. Ondas Sentinel will combine DZYNE and World View under one operating platform. Hartman said the combined Ondas Sentinel organization includes eight U.S. facilities, more than 330,000 square feet of manufacturing capacity, 500 employees and more than 140 engineers. Brock said DZYNE contributes about 145,000 square feet of U.S.-based production capacity. Ondas executives emphasized the role of SkyWeaver, the company’s mission autonomy layer being developed with Palantir. Hartman said SkyWeaver is intended to connect platforms across Ondas’ portfolio and enable tasking, collection and mission autonomy. In response to a question from Sydney Freedberg of Breaking Defense, Hartman said the company does not intend SkyWeaver to be a closed proprietary system, but rather a platform able to ingest data from and task third-party systems. Hartman said SkyWeaver is a joint development program between Ondas and Palantir, with Ondas funding the development. He said Palantir is supporting go-to-market activities and helping ensure Ondas platforms can connect with systems such as Maven. Brock said DZYNE is expected to generate approximately $190 million to $191 million of revenue in 2026 and more than $300 million in 2027. He also said the business is expected to deliver more than 80% compounded annual revenue growth from 2025 through 2028. Ondas raised its 2026 revenue target to more than $525 million, up from the $390 million target it announced in May. Brock said the revised target includes contributions from DZYNE and Omnisys, whose acquisition closed in May. DZYNE has $111 million in backlog and a customer pipeline of more than $1.5 billion, according to Brock. He said Ondas entered the second quarter with approximately $457 million in pro forma backlog and announced more than $150 million of additional orders during the quarter. He also said Ondas expects backlog to expand by $95 million upon closing the Cyberhawk acquisition, which the company expects in the third quarter. In response to a question from Max Michaelis of Lake Street, Brock said the company is seeing gross margins of 40% to 50% for the DZYNE-related profile, while noting Ondas would provide more financial detail on its second-quarter call in August. Management Says Acquisition Pace Will Moderate During the call, Brock said Ondas has been executing a strategy to build a multi-domain autonomous systems company through acquisitions, partnerships and operating scale. Hartman cited recent activity including BIRD Aerosystems, Rotron Aerospace, a Palantir partnership, Mistral, World View and Omnisys. Asked whether the acquisition spree is winding down, Brock said Ondas remains in the early stages of a major adoption cycle for unmanned and autonomous systems, but said the company expects to “moderate the acquisition pace” in the second half and focus on growth, integration and operating leverage. Brock said Ondas’ priorities are to integrate DZYNE, support customers, scale manufacturing, expand recurring revenue and continue investing in technologies that strengthen its competitive position. Ondas Holdings, Inc ONDS develops secure private wireless networking solutions and unmanned aircraft systems tailored to mission-critical industrial applications. Its Ondas Networks division offers the proprietary FullMAX platform, a long-range, high-bandwidth broadband network designed to support real-time data transmission, remote monitoring and IoT deployments across rail, maritime and infrastructure environments. The broadband platform integrates edge-to-cloud architecture to ensure operational resilience and regulatory compliance for transportation and utility operators. The company's Ondas Autonomous Systems segment builds heavy-lift cargo drones and uncrewed aircraft platforms for logistics, pipeline and infrastructure inspection, emergency response and other government and commercial use cases.
