passages: Sep 23, 2026 | By Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President of Microsoft

Microsoft has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991. Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

We are expanding our investments in the Middle East with confidence in the region’s future as it pursues one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region.
From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region:
We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions

Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.

These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available.
We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity

Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows.

Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind

As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible.

Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region.

As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative

Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity

Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation

As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.

A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion

Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.

We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.
We will advance AI for Good research and innovation

Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.
We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy

We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030.

This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.

This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. passages: Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog . The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030.

Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations.

Under the technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, building on existing work with HUMAIN , G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait.

The company cited digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. Microsoft said the partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported where relevant and available by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield.

Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region.

The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

On sustainability, Microsoft said that as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure in the four countries it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, guided by the company’s global goals on carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems. Microsoft said it will also work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities for responsible water stewardship across the region and will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment.

Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative built around digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs intended to help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The company said conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty, and that it will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy.

The company will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, complemented by its sovereign-cloud portfolio. Microsoft also said it is deepening partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in the four countries, and that a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in the four countries will help governments connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft.

Microsoft said it will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. The company’s AI for Good Lab will continue regional research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

Under the people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region.

Existing programs cited by the company include Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings.

Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
Microsoft said it has been part of the region’s journey for more than 35 years and is committed to being a partner for the long term.

extraction.body: Three major press outlets were banned from the White House in part because of… vibes. President Donald Trump’s Justice Department cited a Politico story about bad “vibes” at the Republican Midterm Convention as an example of coverage it factored into its decision to bar CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. The organizations have since sued to regain access . As part of the case, the administration sent unsigned letters to each outlet justifying the ban, including one to Politico citing a Sept. 9 story with the headline, ” ‘The vibes are very bad’ in Texas. ” According to the filing , the outlets have until Friday to contest the administration’s argument. Other apparently objectionable stories from the three outlets included items about the war with Iran ; the United States’ dwindling munitions ; an investigation of a leak in regard to controversial stories about FBI Director Kash Patel ; and a Politico story that included a handout from the Secret Service to Senate Republicans. The Justice Department is hoping Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly will overturn a nearly 50-year-old legal precedent from the case Sherrill v. Knight, which established that press cannot be banned from the White House based on their reporting. “The President determined that Plaintiffs have failed to maintain minimum professional journalistic standards by publishing classified and national security information,” according to a recent Trump Administration legal filing. A lawyer for the outlets slammed the DOJ’s position as “exceptionally weak.” A hearing in the case is slated for Wednesday afternoon. “We look forward to the hearing,” attorney Ted Boutrous told Politico. The press ban led to a boycott by several major news networks. On Monday, Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, and NBC News joined forces and pulled their TV cameras from White House pool. But he, as you mentioned, says that these news outlets write negative news, though he did not specifically say which news stories he is talking about.
This is another troubling escalation from a president that has attacked the First Amendment and the free press in his first administration and now in his second one.
During his first administration, he banned particular reporters, but not entire news outlets, like we're seeing today.
This term, the Associated Press has been removed from the press pool, which PBS is a part of, and the White House has taken over the pool rotation.
The president was asked in the Oval Office today in the afternoon when those badges were being pulled.
We as White House reporters have badges that we wear.
He said he didn't know, but he wants the ban to go as far as it can.
He says that other outlets may be added to this list, Geoff.
Geoff Bennett: And how are the outlets themselves responding to all of this?

Liz Landers: CNN is still reporting from the White House, and they have also released a statement from CNN P.R. saying that they stand by their fair and accurate reporting, and they add that if this ban goes into effect, it will be "an illegal assault on constitutionally protected right to free speech." Politico said that their outlet will continue to defend their First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.
Leading press freedom groups are also reacting to this.

The Freedom of the Press Foundation said in a statement -- quote -- "It's difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the people's house for criticizing the government.
It's also hard to imagine a dumber move." And, Geoff, former Republican White House Press Secretary Ari Fleischer took to X to say that banning certain news outlets is not the solution to this.
He said, instead, try to win the argument with reporters.
So we are seeing Republicans push back on this as well.
Geoff Bennett: OK, Liz Landers, thanks, as always.
extraction.headline: Trump says he's banning 3 outlets from White House in his latest attack on press freedom
extraction.description: President Donald Trump says he is banning three major news outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, from the White House due to what he called "unfavorable coverage." Trump didn't provide details on how the ban would be implemented, but warned he might bar other media outlets as well. White House Correspondent Liz Landers reports on the administration's latest test of First Amendment protections.

The organizations have since sued to regain access . As part of the case, the administration sent unsigned letters to each outlet justifying the ban, including one to Politico citing a Sept. 9 story with the headline, ” ‘The vibes are very bad’ in Texas. ” According to the filing , the outlets have until Friday to contest the administration’s argument. Other apparently objectionable stories from the three outlets included items about the war with Iran ; the United States’ dwindling munitions ; an investigation of a leak in regard to controversial stories about FBI Director Kash Patel ; and a Politico story that included a handout from the Secret Service to Senate Republicans. The Justice Department is hoping Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly will overturn a nearly 50-year-old legal precedent from the case Sherrill v. Knight, which established that press cannot be banned from the White House based on their reporting. “The President determined that Plaintiffs have failed to maintain minimum professional journalistic standards by publishing classified and national security information,” according to a recent Trump Administration legal filing. A lawyer for the outlets slammed the DOJ’s position as “exceptionally weak.” A hearing in the case is slated for Wednesday afternoon. “We look forward to the hearing,” attorney Ted Boutrous told Politico. The press ban led to a boycott by several major news networks. On Monday, Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, and NBC News joined forces and pulled their TV cameras from White House pool. extraction.body: XRP Leads Crypto Losses as Ethereum, Dogecoin Prices Crater Alongside Bitcoin XRP was the worst-performing altcoin among the leading cryptocurrencies Thursday morning, showing a 15% drop over the last 24 hours as markets swing bearish and Bitcoin extends its losses . At the time of writing, XRP was trading for $1.30 after having dropped roughly 28% in the past week, according to crypto price aggregator CoinGecko. An earlier dip to $1.28 marked the lowest price for the Ripple-linked asset since November 2024, when XRP surged in the wake of President Trump's election win. It's also the biggest daily drop of any coin in the top 100 cryptocurrencies by market cap over the last day. Ethereum was recently trading at $1,985 after plunging 6% on the day and losing about 30% of its value in the last week, while original meme coin Dogecoin is down about 8% on the day to $0.09, shedding nearly 19% of its value over the past seven days. BNB was recently changing hands for $666 after having dropped 9% in the past day, losing 23% in the past seven days. Solana had dipped to $85, after falling about 8% in the past day, and was 27% lower than it was this time last week. Bitcoin dove below the $67,000 mark Thursday morning, but was recently trading just above $68,000. The drawdown has resulted in the liquidiation of more than $47 million worth of XRP derivatives contracts. And the bulk of them, nearly $44 million worth, were long on XRP, according to on-chain analytics platform CoinGlass. Overall, more than $1.43 billion worth of crypto positions have been liquidated in the last day. The platform also shows that XRP trading volume has jumped by 57%, with over $11 billion worth of coins changing hands in the past 24 hours. The global crypto market capitalization has now fallen 7.4% on the day to $2.37 trillion after having peaked above $4.2 trillion in September 2025. Meanwhile, XRP treasury firm Evernorth now has a $446 million unrealized loss on its 388,710,631 XRP stash. The company debuted as an XRP treasury in October, saying that its goal was to raise more than $1 billion to buy XRP. It also has backing from Ripple, whose executives are acting as strategic advisors to the firm. In late October, the company spent $947 million buying XRP. It hasn't made another buy since then, but it has watched the value of its XRP holdings drop sharply to approximately $501 million. The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Decrypt . XRP ETF inflows slowed down, but didn't turn red yesterday. The seven spot XRP ETFs that are trading in the U.S. saw $5.9 million in volume and net inflows of $6.9 million on Wednesday, according to an ETF tracker maintained by XRP Insights. Ripple Labs CEO Brad Garlinghouse has been outspoken about the "absolute firestorm of action to get the Market Structure bill passed," but hasn't commented on markets going bearish. Crypto traders are broadly feeling skittish about current market conditions. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index maintained by CoinGlass has dropped to 11, firmly in the "Extreme Fear" category. During the month of January, it very briefly ticked into the greed category when the index peaked at 62, but has been steadily declining since then. extraction.body: XRP Leads Crypto Losses as Ethereum, Dogecoin Prices Crater Alongside Bitcoin XRP was the worst-performing altcoin among the leading cryptocurrencies Thursday morning, showing a 15% drop over the last 24 hours as markets swing bearish and Bitcoin extends its losses . At the time of writing, XRP was trading for $1.30 after having dropped roughly 28% in the past week, according to crypto price aggregator CoinGecko. An earlier dip to $1.28 marked the lowest price for the Ripple-linked asset since November 2024, when XRP surged in the wake of President Trump's election win. It's also the biggest daily drop of any coin in the top 100 cryptocurrencies by market cap over the last day. Ethereum was recently trading at $1,985 after plunging 6% on the day and losing about 30% of its value in the last week, while original meme coin Dogecoin is down about 8% on the day to $0.09, shedding nearly 19% of its value over the past seven days. BNB was recently changing hands for $666 after having dropped 9% in the past day, losing 23% in the past seven days. Solana had dipped to $85, after falling about 8% in the past day, and was 27% lower than it was this time last week. Bitcoin dove below the $67,000 mark Thursday morning, but was recently trading just above $68,000. The drawdown has resulted in the liquidiation of more than $47 million worth of XRP derivatives contracts. And the bulk of them, nearly $44 million worth, were long on XRP, according to on-chain analytics platform CoinGlass. Overall, more than $1.43 billion worth of crypto positions have been liquidated in the last day. The platform also shows that XRP trading volume has jumped by 57%, with over $11 billion worth of coins changing hands in the past 24 hours. The global crypto market capitalization has now fallen 7.4% on the day to $2.37 trillion after having peaked above $4.2 trillion in September 2025. Meanwhile, XRP treasury firm Evernorth now has a $446 million unrealized loss on its 388,710,631 XRP stash. The company debuted as an XRP treasury in October, saying that its goal was to raise more than $1 billion to buy XRP. It also has backing from Ripple, whose executives are acting as strategic advisors to the firm. In late October, the company spent $947 million buying XRP. It hasn't made another buy since then, but it has watched the value of its XRP holdings drop sharply to approximately $501 million. The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Decrypt . XRP ETF inflows slowed down, but didn't turn red yesterday. The seven spot XRP ETFs that are trading in the U.S. saw $5.9 million in volume and net inflows of $6.9 million on Wednesday, according to an ETF tracker maintained by XRP Insights. Ripple Labs CEO Brad Garlinghouse has been outspoken about the "absolute firestorm of action to get the Market Structure bill passed," but hasn't commented on markets going bearish. Crypto traders are broadly feeling skittish about current market conditions. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index maintained by CoinGlass has dropped to 11, firmly in the "Extreme Fear" category. During the month of January, it very briefly ticked into the greed category when the index peaked at 62, but has been steadily declining since then. extraction.body: Feds know of 5 crashes where cars using comma.ai devices hit slow or stopped vehicles. Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 . Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves . At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system. Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam to more than 325 models of car across 27 different brands. More than 30,000 drivers are using openpilot, with more than 402 million miles (650 million km) driven. But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems are able to adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel. At least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle; in one case, it was a first responder’s vehicle, and the resulting crash killed three. Another of the five crashes saw a comma.ai-controlled car hit a vehicle that was merging, hence this preliminary evaluation. NHTSA says it is also interested in which version of the software was running at the time of each crash—at least two involved forks of the main build, including the fatal crash, which was running a version called FrogPilot . extraction.body: Feds know of 5 crashes where cars using comma.ai devices hit slow or stopped vehicles. Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 . Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves . At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system. Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam to more than 325 models of car across 27 different brands. More than 30,000 drivers are using openpilot, with more than 402 million miles (650 million km) driven. But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems are able to adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel. At least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle; in one case, it was a first responder’s vehicle, and the resulting crash killed three. Another of the five crashes saw a comma.ai-controlled car hit a vehicle that was merging, hence this preliminary evaluation. NHTSA says it is also interested in which version of the software was running at the time of each crash—at least two involved forks of the main build, including the fatal crash, which was running a version called FrogPilot . NHTSA said vehicles with Comma devices reportedly struck five stopped or slow-moving vehicles. Comma.ai says the devices that use open source software can allow for hands-free driving and reports more than 30,000 vehicles have logged 402 million miles with the devices.
The system "can accelerate, brake automatically for other vehicles, and steer to follow the road/lane," Comma.ai says.
The company could not immediately be reached for comment but says on its website that it requires "the driver to be alert, pay attention, and be ready to take over at all times."

extraction.body: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access. The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing. It contends that the three news outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ attorney Michael Velchik. The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes. The letters cite a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” The letters also mention news stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia. The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims. The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say. The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.” He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated. First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional. CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds. Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN. On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds. Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual. The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities. Pool coverage is a decades-old system in which one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption Hours after a federal court in California ruled against how President Trump used the National Guard in Los Angeles this summer, Trump touted his use of the National Guard in Washington, D.C., and said he would soon send the troops into Chicago, though he did not say when. "We're going in," Trump said about sending the National Guard to Chicago. The comment came today during a press conference in the Oval Office to announce the new headquarters of the U.S. Space Force . "I'm so very proud of Washington. It serves as the template." Speaking at his own press conference later, Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said the National Guard was not needed or wanted in the city. But he said federal agents were already massing in a nearby military base and predicted they would soon start conducting immigration raids in Latino communities in order to spark demonstrations. "We know, before anything has happened here, that the Trump plan is to use any excuse to deploy armed military personnel to Chicago." Trump deployed some 4,000 guard troops to Los Angeles in June to confront protesters against ICE operations in the city. Only about 300 are still on duty there. Since then, Trump has deployed National Guard troops to Washington, D.C., to assist police, though violent crime rates there were down from recent years, according to Justice Department figures. Earlier Tuesday, a federal judge in San Francisco ruled for the second time that Trump's deployment of the National Guard in Los Angeles violated the law, stating the guard performed law enforcement duties that are prohibited for the military. District Judge Charles R. Breyer delayed the implementation of his ruling until Sept. 12, in which time the Trump administration could appeal. Today's ruling — even if it holds up on appeal — would not impact the use of the guard in other places because it was based on the specific circumstances of what kind of duties the guard has performed in Los Angeles and whether it was overstepping its powers over civilians. "We would have to wait to see what happens because this ruling doesn't say you can never federalize the National Guard," said Jessica Levinson, law professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles. "This ruling says that once the National Guard was on the ground, that they basically they did too much." California Gov. Gavin Newsom celebrated the ruling Tuesday. "Today, the court sided with democracy and the Constitution. No president is a king — not even Trump — and no president can trample a state's power to protect its people," Newsom said in a statement. "As the court today ruled, Trump is breaking the law by 'creating a national police force with the President as its chief.' Trump said today that had he not sent the National Guard to L.A., he'd have to be announcing now that they could not hold the 2028 Olympics there, as are planned. In his ruling today, Breyer said the guard deployment violated the "Posse Comitatus Act," which for nearly 140 years has been in place to keep the military out of civilian law enforcement. The judge took evidence from witnesses in a trial last month about the actions of the guard stationed in L.A., part of a unit called Task Force 51. Attorneys for the state argued with administration attorneys over whether the troops exceeded restrictions on the longstanding ban against U.S. military carrying out law enforcement on civilians. "The record is replete with evidence that Task Force 51 executed domestic law in these prohibited ways," Breyer wrote in a 52-page ruling. He said the troops had gone raids of marijuana farms with federal agents and elsewhere had set up traffic blockades to aid federal agents they were mixed in with. "Bystanders at multiple locations and even federal officials at trial were unable to distinguish Task Force 51 troops from federal law enforcement agents." He cited as another example of law enforcement when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth ordered guard troops to patrol MacArthur Park as a show of force for the federal presence. This is the second time Breyer has ruled against the deployment. He ruled in June that the guard deployment was illegal because there was no rebellion in the city, as Trump had claimed. But a California appeals court ruled on June 19 that there had been incidents of violence against federal agents that justified the guard's deployment and allowed Trump to maintain control of the troops. Breyer's new ruling could be appealed to that court again. Laura Fitzgerald of CapRadio in Sacramento contributed to this story.

Hours after a federal court in California ruled against how President Trump used the National Guard in Los Angeles this summer, Trump touted his use of the National Guard in Washington, D.C., and said he would soon send the troops into Chicago, though he did not say when.

"We're going in," Trump said about sending the National Guard to Chicago. The comment came today during a press conference in the Oval Office to announce the new headquarters of the U.S. Space Force . "I'm so very proud of Washington. It serves as the template."

Speaking at his own press conference later, Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said the National Guard was not needed or wanted in the city. But he said federal agents were already massing in a nearby military base and predicted they would soon start conducting immigration raids in Latino communities in order to spark demonstrations. "We know, before anything has happened here, that the Trump plan is to use any excuse to deploy armed military personnel to Chicago."

Trump deployed some 4,000 guard troops to Los Angeles in June to confront protesters against ICE operations in the city. Only about 300 are still on duty there. Since then, Trump has deployed National Guard troops to Washington, D.C., to assist police, though violent crime rates there were down from recent years, according to Justice Department figures.

Earlier Tuesday, a federal judge in San Francisco ruled for the second time that Trump's deployment of the National Guard in Los Angeles violated the law, stating the guard performed law enforcement duties that are prohibited for the military. District Judge Charles R. Breyer delayed the implementation of his ruling until Sept. 12, in which time the Trump administration could appeal.

Today's ruling — even if it holds up on appeal — would not impact the use of the guard in other places because it was based on the specific circumstances of what kind of duties the guard has performed in Los Angeles and whether it was overstepping its powers over civilians.

"We would have to wait to see what happens because this ruling doesn't say you can never federalize the National Guard," said Jessica Levinson, law professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles. "This ruling says that once the National Guard was on the ground, that they basically they did too much."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom celebrated the ruling Tuesday. "Today, the court sided with democracy and the Constitution. No president is a king — not even Trump — and no president can trample a state's power to protect its people," Newsom said in a statement. "As the court today ruled, Trump is breaking the law by 'creating a national police force with the President as its chief.'
Trump said today that had he not sent the National Guard to L.A., he'd have to be announcing now that they could not hold the 2028 Olympics there, as are planned.
In his ruling today, Breyer said the guard deployment violated the "Posse Comitatus Act," which for nearly 140 years has been in place to keep the military out of civilian law enforcement.

The judge took evidence from witnesses in a trial last month about the actions of the guard stationed in L.A., part of a unit called Task Force 51. Attorneys for the state argued with administration attorneys over whether the troops exceeded restrictions on the longstanding ban against U.S. military carrying out law enforcement on civilians.

"The record is replete with evidence that Task Force 51 executed domestic law in these prohibited ways," Breyer wrote in a 52-page ruling. He said the troops had gone raids of marijuana farms with federal agents and elsewhere had set up traffic blockades to aid federal agents they were mixed in with. "Bystanders at multiple locations and even federal officials at trial were unable to distinguish Task Force 51 troops from federal law enforcement agents."
He cited as another example of law enforcement when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth ordered guard troops to patrol MacArthur Park as a show of force for the federal presence.

This is the second time Breyer has ruled against the deployment. He ruled in June that the guard deployment was illegal because there was no rebellion in the city, as Trump had claimed. But a California appeals court ruled on June 19 that there had been incidents of violence against federal agents that justified the guard's deployment and allowed Trump to maintain control of the troops. Breyer's new ruling could be appealed to that court again.

extraction.body: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access. The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing. It contends that the three news outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ attorney Michael Velchik. The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes. The letters cite a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” The letters also mention news stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia. The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims. The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say. The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.” He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated. First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional. CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds. Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN. On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds. Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual. The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities. Pool coverage is a decades-old system in which one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

extraction.body: Members of the California National Guard and U.S. Marines guard a federal building in June. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption Hours after a federal court in California ruled against how President Trump used the National Guard in Los Angeles this summer, Trump touted his use of the National Guard in Washington, D.C., and said he would soon send the troops into Chicago, though he did not say when. "We're going in," Trump said about sending the National Guard to Chicago. The comment came today during a press conference in the Oval Office to announce the new headquarters of the U.S. Space Force . "I'm so very proud of Washington. It serves as the template." Speaking at his own press conference later, Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said the National Guard was not needed or wanted in the city. But he said federal agents were already massing in a nearby military base and predicted they would soon start conducting immigration raids in Latino communities in order to spark demonstrations. "We know, before anything has happened here, that the Trump plan is to use any excuse to deploy armed military personnel to Chicago." Trump deployed some 4,000 guard troops to Los Angeles in June to confront protesters against ICE operations in the city. Only about 300 are still on duty there. Since then, Trump has deployed National Guard troops to Washington, D.C., to assist police, though violent crime rates there were down from recent years, according to Justice Department figures. Earlier Tuesday, a federal judge in San Francisco ruled for the second time that Trump's deployment of the National Guard in Los Angeles violated the law, stating the guard performed law enforcement duties that are prohibited for the military. District Judge Charles R. Breyer delayed the implementation of his ruling until Sept. 12, in which time the Trump administration could appeal. Today's ruling — even if it holds up on appeal — would not impact the use of the guard in other places because it was based on the specific circumstances of what kind of duties the guard has performed in Los Angeles and whether it was overstepping its powers over civilians. "We would have to wait to see what happens because this ruling doesn't say you can never federalize the National Guard," said Jessica Levinson, law professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles. "This ruling says that once the National Guard was on the ground, that they basically they did too much." California Gov. Gavin Newsom celebrated the ruling Tuesday. "Today, the court sided with democracy and the Constitution. No president is a king — not even Trump — and no president can trample a state's power to protect its people," Newsom said in a statement. "As the court today ruled, Trump is breaking the law by 'creating a national police force with the President as its chief.' Trump said today that had he not sent the National Guard to L.A., he'd have to be announcing now that they could not hold the 2028 Olympics there, as are planned. In his ruling today, Breyer said the guard deployment violated the "Posse Comitatus Act," which for nearly 140 years has been in place to keep the military out of civilian law enforcement. The judge took evidence from witnesses in a trial last month about the actions of the guard stationed in L.A., part of a unit called Task Force 51. Attorneys for the state argued with administration attorneys over whether the troops exceeded restrictions on the longstanding ban against U.S. military carrying out law enforcement on civilians. "The record is replete with evidence that Task Force 51 executed domestic law in these prohibited ways," Breyer wrote in a 52-page ruling. He said the troops had gone raids of marijuana farms with federal agents and elsewhere had set up traffic blockades to aid federal agents they were mixed in with. "Bystanders at multiple locations and even federal officials at trial were unable to distinguish Task Force 51 troops from federal law enforcement agents." He cited as another example of law enforcement when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth ordered guard troops to patrol MacArthur Park as a show of force for the federal presence. This is the second time Breyer has ruled against the deployment. He ruled in June that the guard deployment was illegal because there was no rebellion in the city, as Trump had claimed. But a California appeals court ruled on June 19 that there had been incidents of violence against federal agents that justified the guard's deployment and allowed Trump to maintain control of the troops. Breyer's new ruling could be appealed to that court again. Laura Fitzgerald of CapRadio in Sacramento contributed to this story.

extraction.body: Don’t miss out on securing your ticket savings before they vanish on September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT. Register to grab yours and get a second pass at 50% off. The right introduction can change what happens next for a company. It might lead to your next investor. A customer you’ve been trying to reach. A future hire. A technology partner. Or simply someone solving a problem close enough to yours that the conversation changes how you think about it. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, those people are concentrated in one place. Big events create possibilities. The trick is making them useful. At Disrupt, you can schedule 1:1 meetings through the TechCrunch Events app, which provides AI-powered matchmaking, and you can use the dedicated Networking Lounge across all three days. Alongside that are industry meetups, roundtable sessions , and the conversations that happen when thousands of people building, funding, and scaling technology companies move through the same space. Plus, countless impromptu meetings can happen from running into the right person, anywhere in the venue. Register here to start making intentional connections and save up to $200 before your savings disappear on September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT. There’s a difference between knowing who someone is and actually having a conversation with them. A 15-minute meeting can tell you more about a founder than weeks of following their company online. A conversation with an investor can help you understand what they are really looking for. Meeting another operator can surface an answer to a challenge you assumed was unique to your team. And sometimes the useful conversation is the one you didn’t schedule. The founder sitting next to you before a session. The investor asking the question you were thinking about. The person you meet after a roundtable because you’re both trying to solve the same problem. That proximity matters. You could spend months trying to arrange the individual conversations that become possible over three days at Disrupt. So don’t just build a session schedule. Build a networking schedule. Identify who you want to meet using the event app. Book your one-on-ones. Leave space for the unexpected. Walk the Expo Hall . Stay for the meetups. Talk to the person standing next to you, because one useful conversation can outlast the entire event. Register now to save up to $200 on your ticket and get a second ticket of the same type at 50% off . Or bring a group of four or more to save up to 30%. extraction.body: President Donald Trump returned to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday at and started his address ticking off progress — including adding private sector jobs, stemming illegal migration and curbing crime before turning to a fulsome defense of his decision to start a war with Iran. Trump accused Iran of stalling to make a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and negotiate an endgame to the war until after the midterm elections in the United States “I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” Trump said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind.” Iran’s delegation walked out as Trump railed against Tehran. As he arrived at the UN, Trump briefly spoke to reporters, telling them it was an honor to address the world body before his attention suddenly shifted to his resentments with the news media. Trump over the weekend announced a White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, claiming that their coverage of his presidency was biased. The news outlets have filed a lawsuit to restore their access to White House grounds. Trump snapped at a CNN reporter in the UN scrum. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump said. “You shouldn’t be here.” After his speech to the annual gathering of world leaders, Trump is expected to hold talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and a more informal meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House. The visit to the UN comes when Trump’s foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans’ hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, Trump is making the case in his address that the world is better off for his leadership. “As president of the most extraordinary nation in history,” Trump said. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester.” Iran war to loom large In last year’s address at the UN, Trump claimed the US had “demolished” Iran’s nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities. He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran. Iran can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday. On Sunday, Iran’s military central command said it was informed the US was preparing to restart military operations with the support of regional countries, and warned this would lead ⁠to Tehran’s retaliation “without ⁠limitations and considerations.” “The US needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward,” the senior Iranian official ⁠said, adding the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly is in New York and has full authority to revive diplomacy with the United States. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, who left Tehran for New York on Tuesday morning, will not meet US President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters in New York, the official told Reuters. The Iranian official said ⁠details ⁠on an agreement to end hostilities with Washington can be discussed in New York via mediators, explaining that Tehran’s proposal was delivered to the US through mediators on September 16. “The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said, adding that Tehran would welcome a revival of diplomacy if Washington takes tangible steps. A student opened fire in front of their high school in Türkiye’s western province of Manisa early on Tuesday, wounding at least 11 other pupils, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said. Two of the wounded were in a critical condition, Gurleksaid. The assailant was caught and their mother, father, and grandfather — who owned the weapon used in the attack —have been detained, the minister added. “When the security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any ⁠negligence, any irresponsibility ⁠to be overlooked,” the minister said on X, according to Reuters. “The circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon’s storage, the parents’ obligations regarding care and supervision, and allegations of bullying prior to the incident ⁠are being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles,” Gurlek added. Images and video posted online showed a male figure walking on a street near the school with a rifle in his hands. He was then seen running back from the same street. Video outside the school showed police pushing away families and others outside the premises. The motive for the attack was not immediately clear. The local governor’s office has said ⁠the ⁠attack took place at around 8:00 a.m. (0500 GMT) at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district. Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Türkiye and prompted officials to bring innew security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Before then, the country had not had a history of such attacks. جميع الحقوق محفوظة © شبكة تواصل الإخبارية 2026

sources.title: Trump renames AI 'super intelligence' at UN Assembly as leaders jostle over dangers
passages: United Nations, United States: President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that the US government would rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence" in official communications, as world leaders jostled over how to address the dangers of the fast-advancing technology.

Speaking to the assembly, Trump stood by his firm opposition to regulating AI, while arguing the word "artificial" undersold the technology and voicing hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term.
I am the hoax buster: Trump rejects AI danger warnings

The rebrand is the latest in a series of renamings pursued by the Trump administration, which changed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" via executive order last year and, in August, renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Canada.
China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

extraction.body: Trump defends opposition to AI regulation, says 'artificial' undersells the technology United Nations, United States: President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that the US government would rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence" in official communications, as world leaders jostled over how to address the dangers of the fast-advancing technology. AI has become a major topic at the UN General Assembly after incidents of the technology falling out of the control of humans and warnings by company insiders drew global alarm and calls for better government supervision of the industry. Speaking to the assembly, Trump stood by his firm opposition to regulating AI, while arguing the word "artificial" undersold the technology and voicing hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term. Super Intelligence "sounds much better" and "it's much more accurate," he said. The rebrand is the latest in a series of renamings pursued by the Trump administration, which changed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" via executive order last year and, in August, renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Canada. The US leader also compared the warnings of AI safety advocates to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community. "The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control... artificial intelligence," he said. "Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," he added. "The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster." Ahead of the UN assembly, leaders of more than 20 mostly European countries urged binding safety measures for advanced AI, warning that the technology's development could outpace the ability to control it. AI superpowers China and the United States did not endorse the idea. Speaking at the UN meeting, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain would launch an effort to establish global AI standards during its 2027 G20 presidency, while announcing an AI defense partnership with Washington to detect cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. "We will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe," he said. He earlier revealed London plans to use Britain's role as host of the Group of 20 next year to push for a "single set of global principles and standards" around AI. French President Emmanuel Macron proposed building AI technology independent from the great powers. "I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers," Macron told the UN General Assembly, apparently in reference to China and the US. "Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else." The US-based AI giants themselves are increasingly asking for global coordination on AI safety, with OpenAI's Sam Altman set to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday. Anthropic chief Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue will also participate remotely, a French official said Tuesday. France, which holds the Security Council presidency this month, initiated the meeting and believes AI's threat to international peace and security has not been sufficiently discussed at the UN. UN chief Antonio Guterres, meanwhile, called for the US and China to start a dialogue on the technology's future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War. "Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue," Guterres said in his address to the assembly. "At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks." China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
