Crypto allocations ranged from 0.5% to 13% of investable assets, although most institutions allocated between 1% and 2%. Exposure was spread across spot ETFs, direct ownership, venture investments and hedge funds.
Spot ETFs have also become a major access point. Nearly every institution interviewed either uses them or plans to, citing lower costs and operational complexity.
Bitwise said some institutions use structures that do not appear in 13F filings, meaning public filings may understate overall institutional crypto exposure.

Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan said no institution interviewed identified falling prices as a reason it would sell. Instead, participants pointed to factors such as a breakdown in their investment thesis, regulatory reversal or an industry wide credibility crisis.

The study is based on interviews with 15 institutions and does not represent a broad statistical survey of institutional investors. Bitwise said the findings support its expectation that a majority of institutional investors will hold crypto within five years.

sources.title: Ondas acquires three Israeli companies for $56 million as it builds autonomous defense stack
passages: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare.
The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock.
In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group.

Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year.

Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture.
Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms.
The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception.

Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution.
The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas.
Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally.
The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas.
The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk.

The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies.

extraction.body: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare. The acquisitions of Insignito, Ottopia Defense and Caribou Labs add capabilities spanning passive acoustic drone detection, resilient communications and remote control for unmanned systems, and navigation and communications in environments where GPS and other satellite-based systems are disrupted. The deals include additional contingent consideration of up to $32 million, payable if the businesses meet performance targets through 2028. The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock. Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year. The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas. The company has allocated restricted stock units representing 2,979,063 shares and options to purchase an additional 80,000 shares to the new employees. Taken together, the three acquisitions illustrate the kind of defense technology stack Ondas is attempting to build. Insignito adds another layer to the detection of unmanned aircraft, Ottopia provides the communications and human control needed to operate unmanned systems remotely, while Caribou addresses navigation, positioning and communications when conventional satellite signals are unavailable. Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture. The company says the three technologies range from systems already deployed in active conflict environments to capabilities that can be integrated into its existing platforms in the near term. Insignito, founded in 2022 by entrepreneurs with Air Force backgrounds, specializes in passive acoustic intelligence for counter-drone systems. The technology is designed to complement rather than replace other sensors, including radar, radio-frequency and electro-optical systems. The problem is becoming more significant as drones are increasingly used on battlefields and operators encounter systems designed to avoid traditional detection methods, including fiber-optic-controlled drones. Insignito has also developed several additional technologies around acoustic signatures. The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception. Ottopia Defense addresses a different problem: maintaining the connection between an unmanned vehicle and its human operators when battlefield communications become unreliable. The company develops software and communications infrastructure for transmitting video, telemetry, mission data and commands between unmanned maneuvering platforms, remote operators and command centers. Its system is designed for remote and bandwidth-constrained environments in which communications can be degraded or disrupted. It dynamically manages operational data across available communications channels, with the aim of preserving the flow of information between the vehicle and its operator. Ottopia combines AI-enabled autonomy with ultra-low-latency teleoperation and remote control. This allows operators to supervise multiple unmanned systems, monitor live video and telemetry, and intervene when human judgment or direct control is required. Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms. The acquisition therefore adds the communications and human-control layer to a broader portfolio of autonomous vehicles. Caribou Labs operates in deep tech, specializing in radio-frequency engineering, sensing, communications, positioning and timing for electronic-warfare environments. Its technology is designed to provide positioning and timing without relying on GPS and to maintain resilient communications when digital infrastructure or satellite-based navigation is disrupted. For autonomous systems, losing GNSS signals is not simply a communications problem: it can interfere with a vehicle's ability to determine where it is and how to navigate. Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally. Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution. The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas. The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies. In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group. Earlier this month, it agreed to acquire Israeli Gate Technologies and its Polish manufacturing partner, Bron Technologies, for approximately $205 million, expanding into electronic fuzing systems used in missiles, rockets, UAVs and loitering munitions. Ondas has also acquired U.S. defense technology company DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $876 million, its largest acquisition to date. The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk. The company has been financing the expansion alongside a rapid increase in revenue.

passages: Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous aerial and ground robot intelligence through its Ondas Autonomous Systems ( OAS ) business unit and private wireless solutions through Ondas Networks, and Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG (FWB:HDD) ("Heidelberg"), a global leader in technology and mechanical engineering, today announced the formation of ONBERG Autonomous Systems ("ONBERG"), a joint venture with HD Advanced Technologies GmbH ("HDAT"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Heidelberg.

The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems.

"This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas.

Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments.

HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing.

OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response.
Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing.
These platforms are deployed globally across defense forces, government agencies, and commercial operators to protect sensitive sites, populations, and strategic infrastructure.
The platform is designed to accelerate the development, scaling, and deployment of next-generation robotics, sensing, and defense technologies across allied markets.
Escalate PR ondas@escalatepr.com Preston Grimes Marketing Manager, Ondas Inc. preston.grimes@ondas.com SOURCE: Ondas Holdings Inc.

The company is also focusing on expanding into new business areas such as high-precision plant engineering with integrated control systems, automation technology, robotics, and the growing green technologies sector.

extraction.body: Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous aerial and ground robot intelligence through its Ondas Autonomous Systems ( OAS ) business unit and private wireless solutions through Ondas Networks, and Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG (FWB:HDD) ("Heidelberg"), a global leader in technology and mechanical engineering, today announced the formation of ONBERG Autonomous Systems ("ONBERG"), a joint venture with HD Advanced Technologies GmbH ("HDAT"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Heidelberg. The joint venture formalizes the Memorandum of Understanding signed in December 2025 and establishes a strategic platform to deliver autonomous drone defense and security systems across Germany and Ukraine in first phase. ONBERG is designed to become a European one-stop shop for autonomous drone defense systems protecting critical infrastructure, borders, and national security assets. The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems. "This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas. "Europe is facing an urgent need to protect critical infrastructure, military installations, and civil assets from evolving drone threats. Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing. This partnership enables rapid deployment, industrialized production, and long-term resilience in the European defense ecosystem." Oshri Lugassy, Co-CEO of Ondas Autonomous Systems, added, "ONBERG is structured to deliver a fully integrated, layered autonomous defense architecture tailored for European operational requirements. We will begin with the marketing and deployment of our proven Iron Drone Raider and ISR platforms in Germany and Ukraine and progressively expand into EU markets with localized assembly and manufacturing. By building production, R&D, and integration capabilities in Germany, we are creating a sustainable, scalable platform that supports Europe's long-term strategic autonomy in defense technology." Jürgen Otto, CEO of Heidelberg, commented, "For Heidelberg, the joint venture is the logical next step in the strategic expansion of our dual-use business. Our strategic advantage is our ability to scale up industrially in the heart of Europe, in terms of expertise, experience, skilled workers, manufacturing infrastructure, and investment power. This enables us to ensure fast delivery and innovation, even of high volumes as demanded by today's market." Michael Wellenzohn, CEO of HD Advanced Technologies, added, "With ONBERG, the first true one-stop shop for autonomous security systems in Europe is being created along a joint roadmap. We combine the best of two worlds: OAS's leading drone and sensor technology and 175 years of German engineering expertise and precision mechanics. Thanks to Heidelberg's high vertical range of manufacture, scalable industrial capacities, and expertise in mechatronic precision engineering, we deliver operational excellence at the highest level. HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing. The joint roadmap includes permanent establishment of sales, development, and industrial production capabilities, supporting high-volume demand and contributing to the development of a sovereign European defense industry. Ondas continues to expand its role as a defense technology prime delivering scalable ISR and counter-UAS systems. The joint venture strengthens Ondas' regional industrial footprint and advances its strategy of integrating air, ground, sensing, and interception capabilities into unified operational architectures across NATO and allied markets. Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) is a leading provider of autonomous systems, robotics, and mission-critical connectivity solutions for defense, security, and industrial markets. Through its business units (Ondas Autonomous Systems, Ondas Capital and Ondas Networks), the Company develops and deploys integrated technologies that deliver advanced sensing, mobility, and communications capabilities for complex operational environments. Ondas Autonomous Systems (OAS) delivers a portfolio of AI-enabled air and ground robotic platforms and counter-UAS technologies designed to support defense, homeland security, and critical infrastructure protection missions worldwide. OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response. These platforms are deployed globally across defense forces, government agencies, and commercial operators to protect sensitive sites, populations, and strategic infrastructure. Ondas Capital focuses on strategic investments, partnerships, and advisory initiatives that support the growth of the global autonomous systems ecosystem. The platform is designed to accelerate the development, scaling, and deployment of next-generation robotics, sensing, and defense technologies across allied markets. Ondas Networks provides mission-critical wireless connectivity through its FullMAX platform, a software-defined broadband solution based on the IEEE 802.16t standard. Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments. extraction.body: Ondas ONDS said it has acquired DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $875 million, marking what Chairman and CEO Eric Brock described as a transformational step in building a scaled autonomous defense and security platform. Speaking on an investor event call, Brock said the deal includes $200 million in cash and approximately $675 million in Ondas equity. He said the acquisition closed concurrently with signing on July 2, allowing integration to begin immediately. DZYNE shareholders, led by majority owner Highlander Partners, will become among Ondas’ largest stockholders, and Highlander has locked up more than half of the shares it received for six months, according to Brock. “This is not a financial acquisition,” Brock said. “It is a strategic combination designed to create a larger, stronger, and more competitive autonomous defense company.” Brock said DZYNE brings operational products, a U.S.-based manufacturing base, customer relationships across defense agencies and allied militaries, and nearly 120 engineers. He said the acquisition expands Ondas’ position in persistent intelligence, aerial security, counter-drone systems, autonomous effects and AI-enabled mission intelligence. DZYNE’s portfolio spans three core franchises, according to the company presentation: Matt McCue, founder and CEO of DZYNE and incoming chief technology officer of Ondas Sentinel, said Ultra provides more than three days of endurance at more than 25,000 feet, while LEAP provides more than a day of endurance at 17,000 feet. He said both platforms are in operational use with U.S. and allied partners. McCue said IonStrike was developed from concept to demonstrated capability in six months to address threats such as the Shahed-136 drone. He also highlighted Dronebuster and Sawtooth as soft-kill counter-UAS systems, and said DZYNE is working on a long-range electronic attack solution and lidar detection capability. Ryan Hartman, CEO of Ondas Sentinel, said DZYNE fills a gap between Ondas’ lower-altitude unmanned systems and stratospheric assets, adding Group 4 and Group 5 long-endurance UAS capabilities. Ondas Sentinel will combine DZYNE and World View under one operating platform. Hartman said the combined Ondas Sentinel organization includes eight U.S. facilities, more than 330,000 square feet of manufacturing capacity, 500 employees and more than 140 engineers. Brock said DZYNE contributes about 145,000 square feet of U.S.-based production capacity. Ondas executives emphasized the role of SkyWeaver, the company’s mission autonomy layer being developed with Palantir. Hartman said SkyWeaver is intended to connect platforms across Ondas’ portfolio and enable tasking, collection and mission autonomy. In response to a question from Sydney Freedberg of Breaking Defense, Hartman said the company does not intend SkyWeaver to be a closed proprietary system, but rather a platform able to ingest data from and task third-party systems. Hartman said SkyWeaver is a joint development program between Ondas and Palantir, with Ondas funding the development. He said Palantir is supporting go-to-market activities and helping ensure Ondas platforms can connect with systems such as Maven. Brock said DZYNE is expected to generate approximately $190 million to $191 million of revenue in 2026 and more than $300 million in 2027. He also said the business is expected to deliver more than 80% compounded annual revenue growth from 2025 through 2028. Ondas raised its 2026 revenue target to more than $525 million, up from the $390 million target it announced in May. Brock said the revised target includes contributions from DZYNE and Omnisys, whose acquisition closed in May. DZYNE has $111 million in backlog and a customer pipeline of more than $1.5 billion, according to Brock. He said Ondas entered the second quarter with approximately $457 million in pro forma backlog and announced more than $150 million of additional orders during the quarter. He also said Ondas expects backlog to expand by $95 million upon closing the Cyberhawk acquisition, which the company expects in the third quarter. In response to a question from Max Michaelis of Lake Street, Brock said the company is seeing gross margins of 40% to 50% for the DZYNE-related profile, while noting Ondas would provide more financial detail on its second-quarter call in August. Management Says Acquisition Pace Will Moderate During the call, Brock said Ondas has been executing a strategy to build a multi-domain autonomous systems company through acquisitions, partnerships and operating scale. Hartman cited recent activity including BIRD Aerosystems, Rotron Aerospace, a Palantir partnership, Mistral, World View and Omnisys. Asked whether the acquisition spree is winding down, Brock said Ondas remains in the early stages of a major adoption cycle for unmanned and autonomous systems, but said the company expects to “moderate the acquisition pace” in the second half and focus on growth, integration and operating leverage. Brock said Ondas’ priorities are to integrate DZYNE, support customers, scale manufacturing, expand recurring revenue and continue investing in technologies that strengthen its competitive position. Ondas Holdings, Inc ONDS develops secure private wireless networking solutions and unmanned aircraft systems tailored to mission-critical industrial applications. Its Ondas Networks division offers the proprietary FullMAX platform, a long-range, high-bandwidth broadband network designed to support real-time data transmission, remote monitoring and IoT deployments across rail, maritime and infrastructure environments. The broadband platform integrates edge-to-cloud architecture to ensure operational resilience and regulatory compliance for transportation and utility operators. The company's Ondas Autonomous Systems segment builds heavy-lift cargo drones and uncrewed aircraft platforms for logistics, pipeline and infrastructure inspection, emergency response and other government and commercial use cases. Matt McCue, founder and CEO of DZYNE and incoming chief technology officer of Ondas Sentinel, said Ultra provides more than three days of endurance at more than 25,000 feet, while LEAP provides more than a day of endurance at 17,000 feet. He said both platforms are in operational use with U.S. and allied partners.

McCue said IonStrike was developed from concept to demonstrated capability in six months to address threats such as the Shahed-136 drone. He also highlighted Dronebuster and Sawtooth as soft-kill counter-UAS systems, and said DZYNE is working on a long-range electronic attack solution and lidar detection capability.

Ryan Hartman, CEO of Ondas Sentinel, said DZYNE fills a gap between Ondas’ lower-altitude unmanned systems and stratospheric assets, adding Group 4 and Group 5 long-endurance UAS capabilities. Ondas Sentinel will combine DZYNE and World View under one operating platform.

Ondas executives emphasized the role of SkyWeaver, the company’s mission autonomy layer being developed with Palantir. In response to a question from Sydney Freedberg of Breaking Defense, Hartman said the company does not intend SkyWeaver to be a closed proprietary system, but rather a platform able to ingest data from and task third-party systems.

Hartman said SkyWeaver is a joint development program between Ondas and Palantir, with Ondas funding the development. He said Palantir is supporting go-to-market activities and helping ensure Ondas platforms can connect with systems such as Maven.

Brock said DZYNE is expected to generate approximately $190 million to $191 million of revenue in 2026 and more than $300 million in 2027. He also said the business is expected to deliver more than 80% compounded annual revenue growth from 2025 through 2028.

In response to a question from Max Michaelis of Lake Street, Brock said the company is seeing gross margins of 40% to 50% for the DZYNE-related profile, while noting Ondas would provide more financial detail on its second-quarter call in August.

During the call, Brock said Ondas has been executing a strategy to build a multi-domain autonomous systems company through acquisitions, partnerships and operating scale. Hartman cited recent activity including BIRD Aerosystems, Rotron Aerospace, a Palantir partnership, Mistral, World View and Omnisys.

Asked whether the acquisition spree is winding down, Brock said Ondas remains in the early stages of a major adoption cycle for unmanned and autonomous systems, but said the company expects to “moderate the acquisition pace” in the second half and focus on growth, integration and operating leverage.
Brock said Ondas’ priorities are to integrate DZYNE, support customers, scale manufacturing, expand recurring revenue and continue investing in technologies that strengthen its competitive position.

The broadband platform integrates edge-to-cloud architecture to ensure operational resilience and regulatory compliance for transportation and utility operators.

coreStoryFacts.text: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare.
The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock.
In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group.

Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year.

Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture.
Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms.
The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception.

Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution.
The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas.
Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally.
The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas.
The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk.

The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies.

Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous aerial and ground robot intelligence through its Ondas Autonomous Systems ( OAS ) business unit and private wireless solutions through Ondas Networks, and Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG (FWB:HDD) ("Heidelberg"), a global leader in technology and mechanical engineering, today announced the formation of ONBERG Autonomous Systems ("ONBERG"), a joint venture with HD Advanced Technologies GmbH ("HDAT"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Heidelberg.

The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems.

"This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas.

Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments.

HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing.

OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response.
Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing.

The company is also focusing on expanding into new business areas such as high-precision plant engineering with integrated control systems, automation technology, robotics, and the growing green technologies sector.
Ondas raised its 2026 revenue target to more than $525 million, up from the $390 million target it announced in May.
Brock said the revised target includes contributions from DZYNE and Omnisys, whose acquisition closed in May.

Ondas ONDS said it has acquired DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $875 million, marking what Chairman and CEO Eric Brock described as a transformational step in building a scaled autonomous defense and security platform.

extraction.body: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare. The acquisitions of Insignito, Ottopia Defense and Caribou Labs add capabilities spanning passive acoustic drone detection, resilient communications and remote control for unmanned systems, and navigation and communications in environments where GPS and other satellite-based systems are disrupted. The deals include additional contingent consideration of up to $32 million, payable if the businesses meet performance targets through 2028. The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock. Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year. The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas. The company has allocated restricted stock units representing 2,979,063 shares and options to purchase an additional 80,000 shares to the new employees. Taken together, the three acquisitions illustrate the kind of defense technology stack Ondas is attempting to build. Insignito adds another layer to the detection of unmanned aircraft, Ottopia provides the communications and human control needed to operate unmanned systems remotely, while Caribou addresses navigation, positioning and communications when conventional satellite signals are unavailable. Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture. The company says the three technologies range from systems already deployed in active conflict environments to capabilities that can be integrated into its existing platforms in the near term. Insignito, founded in 2022 by entrepreneurs with Air Force backgrounds, specializes in passive acoustic intelligence for counter-drone systems. The technology is designed to complement rather than replace other sensors, including radar, radio-frequency and electro-optical systems. The problem is becoming more significant as drones are increasingly used on battlefields and operators encounter systems designed to avoid traditional detection methods, including fiber-optic-controlled drones. Insignito has also developed several additional technologies around acoustic signatures. The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception. Ottopia Defense addresses a different problem: maintaining the connection between an unmanned vehicle and its human operators when battlefield communications become unreliable. The company develops software and communications infrastructure for transmitting video, telemetry, mission data and commands between unmanned maneuvering platforms, remote operators and command centers. Its system is designed for remote and bandwidth-constrained environments in which communications can be degraded or disrupted. It dynamically manages operational data across available communications channels, with the aim of preserving the flow of information between the vehicle and its operator. Ottopia combines AI-enabled autonomy with ultra-low-latency teleoperation and remote control. This allows operators to supervise multiple unmanned systems, monitor live video and telemetry, and intervene when human judgment or direct control is required. Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms. The acquisition therefore adds the communications and human-control layer to a broader portfolio of autonomous vehicles. Caribou Labs operates in deep tech, specializing in radio-frequency engineering, sensing, communications, positioning and timing for electronic-warfare environments. Its technology is designed to provide positioning and timing without relying on GPS and to maintain resilient communications when digital infrastructure or satellite-based navigation is disrupted. For autonomous systems, losing GNSS signals is not simply a communications problem: it can interfere with a vehicle's ability to determine where it is and how to navigate. Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally. Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution. The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas. The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies. In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group. Earlier this month, it agreed to acquire Israeli Gate Technologies and its Polish manufacturing partner, Bron Technologies, for approximately $205 million, expanding into electronic fuzing systems used in missiles, rockets, UAVs and loitering munitions. Ondas has also acquired U.S. defense technology company DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $876 million, its largest acquisition to date. The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk. The company has been financing the expansion alongside a rapid increase in revenue.

The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems. "This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas. Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments. HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing. OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response. Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing. These platforms are deployed globally across defense forces, government agencies, and commercial operators to protect sensitive sites, populations, and strategic infrastructure. The platform is designed to accelerate the development, scaling, and deployment of next-generation robotics, sensing, and defense technologies across allied markets. Escalate PR ondas@escalatepr.com Preston Grimes Marketing Manager, Ondas Inc. preston.grimes@ondas.com SOURCE: Ondas Holdings Inc. The company is also focusing on expanding into new business areas such as high-precision plant engineering with integrated control systems, automation technology, robotics, and the growing green technologies sector.

extraction.body: Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous aerial and ground robot intelligence through its Ondas Autonomous Systems ( OAS ) business unit and private wireless solutions through Ondas Networks, and Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG (FWB:HDD) ("Heidelberg"), a global leader in technology and mechanical engineering, today announced the formation of ONBERG Autonomous Systems ("ONBERG"), a joint venture with HD Advanced Technologies GmbH ("HDAT"), a wholly owned subsidiary of Heidelberg. The joint venture formalizes the Memorandum of Understanding signed in December 2025 and establishes a strategic platform to deliver autonomous drone defense and security systems across Germany and Ukraine in first phase. ONBERG is designed to become a European one-stop shop for autonomous drone defense systems protecting critical infrastructure, borders, and national security assets. The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems. "This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas. "Europe is facing an urgent need to protect critical infrastructure, military installations, and civil assets from evolving drone threats. Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing. This partnership enables rapid deployment, industrialized production, and long-term resilience in the European defense ecosystem." Oshri Lugassy, Co-CEO of Ondas Autonomous Systems, added, "ONBERG is structured to deliver a fully integrated, layered autonomous defense architecture tailored for European operational requirements. We will begin with the marketing and deployment of our proven Iron Drone Raider and ISR platforms in Germany and Ukraine and progressively expand into EU markets with localized assembly and manufacturing. By building production, R&D, and integration capabilities in Germany, we are creating a sustainable, scalable platform that supports Europe's long-term strategic autonomy in defense technology." Jürgen Otto, CEO of Heidelberg, commented, "For Heidelberg, the joint venture is the logical next step in the strategic expansion of our dual-use business. Our strategic advantage is our ability to scale up industrially in the heart of Europe, in terms of expertise, experience, skilled workers, manufacturing infrastructure, and investment power. This enables us to ensure fast delivery and innovation, even of high volumes as demanded by today's market." Michael Wellenzohn, CEO of HD Advanced Technologies, added, "With ONBERG, the first true one-stop shop for autonomous security systems in Europe is being created along a joint roadmap. We combine the best of two worlds: OAS's leading drone and sensor technology and 175 years of German engineering expertise and precision mechanics. Thanks to Heidelberg's high vertical range of manufacture, scalable industrial capacities, and expertise in mechatronic precision engineering, we deliver operational excellence at the highest level. HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing. The joint roadmap includes permanent establishment of sales, development, and industrial production capabilities, supporting high-volume demand and contributing to the development of a sovereign European defense industry. Ondas continues to expand its role as a defense technology prime delivering scalable ISR and counter-UAS systems. The joint venture strengthens Ondas' regional industrial footprint and advances its strategy of integrating air, ground, sensing, and interception capabilities into unified operational architectures across NATO and allied markets. Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) is a leading provider of autonomous systems, robotics, and mission-critical connectivity solutions for defense, security, and industrial markets. Through its business units (Ondas Autonomous Systems, Ondas Capital and Ondas Networks), the Company develops and deploys integrated technologies that deliver advanced sensing, mobility, and communications capabilities for complex operational environments. Ondas Autonomous Systems (OAS) delivers a portfolio of AI-enabled air and ground robotic platforms and counter-UAS technologies designed to support defense, homeland security, and critical infrastructure protection missions worldwide. OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response. These platforms are deployed globally across defense forces, government agencies, and commercial operators to protect sensitive sites, populations, and strategic infrastructure. Ondas Capital focuses on strategic investments, partnerships, and advisory initiatives that support the growth of the global autonomous systems ecosystem. The platform is designed to accelerate the development, scaling, and deployment of next-generation robotics, sensing, and defense technologies across allied markets. Ondas Networks provides mission-critical wireless connectivity through its FullMAX platform, a software-defined broadband solution based on the IEEE 802.16t standard. Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments. extraction.body: Ondas ONDS said it has acquired DZYNE Technologies in a transaction valued at approximately $875 million, marking what Chairman and CEO Eric Brock described as a transformational step in building a scaled autonomous defense and security platform. Speaking on an investor event call, Brock said the deal includes $200 million in cash and approximately $675 million in Ondas equity. He said the acquisition closed concurrently with signing on July 2, allowing integration to begin immediately. DZYNE shareholders, led by majority owner Highlander Partners, will become among Ondas’ largest stockholders, and Highlander has locked up more than half of the shares it received for six months, according to Brock. “This is not a financial acquisition,” Brock said. “It is a strategic combination designed to create a larger, stronger, and more competitive autonomous defense company.” Brock said DZYNE brings operational products, a U.S.-based manufacturing base, customer relationships across defense agencies and allied militaries, and nearly 120 engineers. He said the acquisition expands Ondas’ position in persistent intelligence, aerial security, counter-drone systems, autonomous effects and AI-enabled mission intelligence. DZYNE’s portfolio spans three core franchises, according to the company presentation: Matt McCue, founder and CEO of DZYNE and incoming chief technology officer of Ondas Sentinel, said Ultra provides more than three days of endurance at more than 25,000 feet, while LEAP provides more than a day of endurance at 17,000 feet. He said both platforms are in operational use with U.S. and allied partners. McCue said IonStrike was developed from concept to demonstrated capability in six months to address threats such as the Shahed-136 drone. He also highlighted Dronebuster and Sawtooth as soft-kill counter-UAS systems, and said DZYNE is working on a long-range electronic attack solution and lidar detection capability. Ryan Hartman, CEO of Ondas Sentinel, said DZYNE fills a gap between Ondas’ lower-altitude unmanned systems and stratospheric assets, adding Group 4 and Group 5 long-endurance UAS capabilities. Ondas Sentinel will combine DZYNE and World View under one operating platform. Hartman said the combined Ondas Sentinel organization includes eight U.S. facilities, more than 330,000 square feet of manufacturing capacity, 500 employees and more than 140 engineers. Brock said DZYNE contributes about 145,000 square feet of U.S.-based production capacity. Ondas executives emphasized the role of SkyWeaver, the company’s mission autonomy layer being developed with Palantir. Hartman said SkyWeaver is intended to connect platforms across Ondas’ portfolio and enable tasking, collection and mission autonomy. In response to a question from Sydney Freedberg of Breaking Defense, Hartman said the company does not intend SkyWeaver to be a closed proprietary system, but rather a platform able to ingest data from and task third-party systems. Hartman said SkyWeaver is a joint development program between Ondas and Palantir, with Ondas funding the development. He said Palantir is supporting go-to-market activities and helping ensure Ondas platforms can connect with systems such as Maven. Brock said DZYNE is expected to generate approximately $190 million to $191 million of revenue in 2026 and more than $300 million in 2027. He also said the business is expected to deliver more than 80% compounded annual revenue growth from 2025 through 2028. Ondas raised its 2026 revenue target to more than $525 million, up from the $390 million target it announced in May. Brock said the revised target includes contributions from DZYNE and Omnisys, whose acquisition closed in May. DZYNE has $111 million in backlog and a customer pipeline of more than $1.5 billion, according to Brock. He said Ondas entered the second quarter with approximately $457 million in pro forma backlog and announced more than $150 million of additional orders during the quarter. He also said Ondas expects backlog to expand by $95 million upon closing the Cyberhawk acquisition, which the company expects in the third quarter. In response to a question from Max Michaelis of Lake Street, Brock said the company is seeing gross margins of 40% to 50% for the DZYNE-related profile, while noting Ondas would provide more financial detail on its second-quarter call in August. Management Says Acquisition Pace Will Moderate During the call, Brock said Ondas has been executing a strategy to build a multi-domain autonomous systems company through acquisitions, partnerships and operating scale. Hartman cited recent activity including BIRD Aerosystems, Rotron Aerospace, a Palantir partnership, Mistral, World View and Omnisys. Asked whether the acquisition spree is winding down, Brock said Ondas remains in the early stages of a major adoption cycle for unmanned and autonomous systems, but said the company expects to “moderate the acquisition pace” in the second half and focus on growth, integration and operating leverage. Brock said Ondas’ priorities are to integrate DZYNE, support customers, scale manufacturing, expand recurring revenue and continue investing in technologies that strengthen its competitive position. Ondas Holdings, Inc ONDS develops secure private wireless networking solutions and unmanned aircraft systems tailored to mission-critical industrial applications. Its Ondas Networks division offers the proprietary FullMAX platform, a long-range, high-bandwidth broadband network designed to support real-time data transmission, remote monitoring and IoT deployments across rail, maritime and infrastructure environments. The broadband platform integrates edge-to-cloud architecture to ensure operational resilience and regulatory compliance for transportation and utility operators. The company's Ondas Autonomous Systems segment builds heavy-lift cargo drones and uncrewed aircraft platforms for logistics, pipeline and infrastructure inspection, emergency response and other government and commercial use cases. story.title: Ondas Acquires Three Defense Technology Businesses to Expand Its Integrated Autonomous Defense Systems Platform - Ondas Holdings

facts.text: U.S.-listed defense technology company Ondas is continuing its aggressive acquisition spree in Israel, acquiring three defense technology businesses for a total of $56 million as it seeks to assemble a broader technology stack for autonomous warfare.
The initial $56 million consideration will be paid in cash or Ondas stock.
In August, Ondas agreed to acquire Aran Defense for $33 million, adding development and manufacturing capabilities to the group.

Based on Ondas's forecasts, the initial purchase price represents less than three times the three companies' expected combined revenue in 2027, implying projected revenue of nearly $19 million that year.

Ondas describes the strategy as a “System of Systems” approach, in which platforms, sensors, communications, software and command-and-control capabilities are integrated across a broader autonomous defense architecture.
Ondas plans to integrate the technology into its unmanned ground systems, including Iron Wave, one of the company's autonomous ground platforms.
The combination gives Ondas capabilities across several stages of the drone-defense process, from detection and tracking to mission planning, signature reduction and, eventually, interception.

Ondas intends to use Caribou's capabilities across its aerial, ground and command platforms, adding another component to what it describes as an end-to-end autonomy and resilience stack spanning connectivity, navigation, identification and mission execution.
The acquisitions will also bring 37 employees into Ondas.
Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments, according to Ondas, and the company says it has a pipeline of potential customers globally.
The purchases are the latest in an acquisition campaign that has rapidly changed the scale and composition of Ondas.
The deal followed purchases including Israeli mission-management software company Omnisys and Scotland-based Cyberhawk.

The company has assembled a portfolio of more than 15 businesses over the past two years, with acquisitions spanning drones, robotics, counter-drone systems, intelligence, communications and other defense technologies.

The joint venture will combine OAS' battle-proven counter-UAS, ISR, and autonomous security technologies with Heidelberg's 175 years of German engineering excellence, scalable industrial manufacturing capabilities, and established European production infrastructure, including expansion of the Brandenburg an der Havel site into a center of excellence for autonomous defense systems.

"This joint venture represents a significant step in Ondas' strategy to localize production and strengthen sovereign defense capabilities within allied nations," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas.

Together, Ondas' technologies combine autonomous systems, advanced sensing, and resilient connectivity to deliver integrated operational capabilities that enhance security, efficiency, and decision-making in some of the world's most demanding environments.

HDAT and OAS are thus positioning themselves as strong partners in building a sovereign national defense industry." ONBERG plans to industrialize production in Germany using European supply chains, expanding from distribution and integration to localized assembly and full manufacturing.

OAS solutions include autonomous drone platforms, robotic ground systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced propulsion and unmanned aircraft capabilities, autonomous engineering and demining capabilities, and integrated sensing systems that enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, security, and operational response.
Through ONBERG, we are combining American-Israeli high-tech defense innovation with German industrial scale and precision manufacturing.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. As per a CNN report citing these letters, Politico’s entry was banned due to its reporting on Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions. About The Dispute: The dispute began last week when Trump barred journalists from the three outlets from entering the White House grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing that the restrictions violate their First Amendment rights. At the same time, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC suspended their pooled television coverage of Trump after the White House prevented CNN from carrying out its scheduled role as pool representative during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump's Clarification: Trump strongly defended the decision in multiple Truth Social posts, rejecting the allegations that the White House was attacking the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” He described the coverage from the three outlets as “corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” and said it was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump also argued that the media organizations should not automatically receive access to the White House.

The Justice Department has urged a federal court to uphold President Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, arguing White House access is not a public right. The United States Department of Justice has formally defended President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major news organizations from the White House, arguing in a late-night court filing that presidential access is a "privilege—not a right." The legal maneuver seeks to uphold the administration's revocation of press credentials for journalists from CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, citing severe national security concerns and alleged breaches of professional decorum. The filing, submitted to a federal court in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday evening, arrived just hours before an emergency hearing concerning the media outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. The news organizations are suing the Trump administration to immediately restore their White House access, characterizing the ban as a flagrant violation of their First Amendment rights. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power. In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office. "The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information." The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom. The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous. For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict. The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent. The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. Legal representatives for the networks argue that the cited articles relied on corroborated sources and standard journalistic practices, portraying the administration's national security claims as a pretext for punishing unfavorable coverage. The current controversy erupted on Friday when Trump announced the bans via a post on his Truth Social platform, declaring the move "effective immediately." He justified the decision by accusing the networks of reporting "fiction and lies" and suggested that other media organizations might face similar expulsions. Press freedom advocates have condemned the bans as a retaliatory tactic designed to chill independent journalism. Legal experts note that federal courts have historically sided with the press when the Trump administration previously attempted to revoke individual credentials, such as the high-profile disputes involving CNN's Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during his first term. In those instances, courts ruled that the administration could not arbitrarily revoke credentials without providing rigorous due process. However, the Justice Department is now attempting to establish a broader legal precedent, leaning heavily on the argument that the physical security of the White House supersedes general press access rights. The government explicitly argued that the bans were not retaliatory, claiming that the administration would have taken the same action regarding the classified leaks regardless of the outlets' broader editorial criticism of the president. The outcome of Wednesday's emergency hearing will carry significant implications for the functioning of the White House press corps. Without a traveling pool representative from CNN, the television network pool was left empty during the president's movements earlier in the week, disrupting the standard distribution of presidential activities to the broader public. As the legal proceedings advance, the confrontation highlights a critical constitutional tension. While the government insists on its right to control the physical perimeter of the executive branch, media organizations warn that allowing a president to unilaterally ban specific outlets based on their reporting fundamentally undermines the democratic principle of a free and unhindered press. Reporters from those news organizations were stripped of their press credentials, also called "hard passes," denying them access to the White House grounds."Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Justice Department lawyers wrote.The Trump administration argued the president's ban complies with the First Amendment, because the government has at least two "compelling reasons" for denying the reporters' access: enforcing "minimum standards of professionalism" for the press and protecting classified information."The President believes basic journalistic standards require calling, asking for comment, and providing a reasonable opportunity for a response," they said. "At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information."The Justice Department also submitted to the court letters from the White House press office, dated Tuesday, to each of the three outlets notifying them that the president decided to revoke their journalists' hard passes. The letters claim that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to respond to its claims.The letters appear designed to address the news outlets' claims that the ban deprived them of due process, since their reporters didn't receive advance notice that they would be denied access to the White House and an opportunity to be heard before revoking their credentials."The President provided no notice that he would immediately deny news organizations whose reporting he dislikes access to the White House grounds," lawyers for the organizations said in a filing. "His standard for denying access is arbitrary and vague — indeed, it can hardly be called a standard at all."The Justice Department's response comes ahead of a hearing, set for Wednesday afternoon, during which a judge will consider whether to order the White House to restore the media organizations' credentials and access. Notably, Trump has a long history of describing reporting that portrays him in a negative light as “fake,” even when the reporting is factual.
In a subsequent post over the weekend , Trump again alleged that the news agencies utilized fake reports, claiming that such reporting is “a threat to our National Security” that “must be stopped.”

Trump’s posts were cited by the DOJ in a legal filing responding to a joint lawsuit from CNN , MS NOW , and Politico . The suit seeks to put a stay on Trump’s attempt to block their access to the White House.
The DOJ argues that such access is a “privilege” that news agencies enjoy, and states that presidents have the legal authority to block whoever they want.

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ filing forcefully claims , adding that Trump can enforce “minimum standards for bona fide journalists and safeguarding national security information.”

The filing also argues that these news orgs were unprofessional through their use of anonymous sources to publish stories about the White House — a practice that has existed for decades, if not longer, and which Trump himself has utilized in the past to criticize his political opponents.

Attempting to prove Trump’s order should remain in place, the filing cites CNN’s reporting on a bunker underneath Trump’s planned East Wing ballroom; MS NOW’s reporting on the White House’s investigation into leaks; and Politico’s reporting on Secret Service funds being used to help pay for security improvements in the planned ballroom.

It is unclear how the outlets’ reporting on these subjects detrimentally affects national security — indeed, the reports contain information that the American public may have a vested interest in. Observers also noted that some of the reports cited in the filing are a matter of public record.
Ryan Goodman, co-editor-in-chief of Just Security , described the reporting cited in the filing as “core First Amendment protected reporting.”

The DOJ “gives an example of ‘In August 2026, MSNOW claimed that the Iran conflict had ‘significantly depleted’ the US military’s munitions supply.’ What was the MSNOW source for that claim? This document, which is published in the Federal Register,” Goodman wrote, sharing the document in his Bluesky post .
“The United Nations allowed us in, sir,” Collins retorted.
“You should not be here covering me,” Trump said. He then wrongly claimed that the network had said it would no longer be reporting on him due to the ban.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. As per a CNN report citing these letters, Politico’s entry was banned due to its reporting on Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions. About The Dispute: The dispute began last week when Trump barred journalists from the three outlets from entering the White House grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing that the restrictions violate their First Amendment rights. At the same time, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC suspended their pooled television coverage of Trump after the White House prevented CNN from carrying out its scheduled role as pool representative during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump's Clarification: Trump strongly defended the decision in multiple Truth Social posts, rejecting the allegations that the White House was attacking the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” He described the coverage from the three outlets as “corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” and said it was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump also argued that the media organizations should not automatically receive access to the White House.
